Conjecture D implies that the category of motives with numerical equivalence is semisimple abelian, a result proven by Jannsen (1992). The Tate conjecture, predicting that the cycle class map to Galois-invariant classes in ℓ-adic cohomology is surjective, is the ℓ-adic analogue of the Hodge conjecture. For abelian varieties, the Tate conjecture is known in many cases (Faltings, Zarhin). Mixed motives, extending to non-smooth or non-proper varieties, were constructed by Voevodsky (1995) using the derived category of motivic complexes DMk, yielding a triangulated category with a t-structure whose heart is the conjectural abelian category of mixed motives. The motivic Galois group, the automorphism group of the fiber functor, controls the relations among periods of algebraic varieties. The period conjecture of Grothendieck asserts that the transcendence degree of the period field equals the dimension of the motivic Galois group. Examiners often test the distinction between adequate equivalence relations and the role of the Lefschetz standard conjecture in proving the semisimplicity of the category of motives.

The Theory of Intersection Cohomology and the Decomposition Theorem

Intersection cohomology, introduced by Goresky and MacPherson (1980), provides a cohomology theory for singular spaces that satisfies Poincaré duality. For a stratified pseudomanifold X of dimension n, the intersection cohomology groups IHk(X; ℚ) are defined using chains that intersect strata in a controlled way, governed by a perversity function p. The middle perversity m(k) = ⌊(k−2)/2⌋ yields self-dual groups. The Decomposition Theorem (Beilinson–Bernstein–Deligne–Gabber, 1982) is the central result: for a proper map f : X → Y of complex algebraic varieties with X smooth, the derived pushforward Rf*ℚX[n] splits in the derived category of constructible sheaves on Y as a direct sum of shifted intersection cohomology complexes of local systems on strata: Rf*ℚX[n] ≅ ⊕i ⊕α ICZα(Lα)[−i]. This implies the hard Lefschetz theorem and Hodge–Riemann bilinear relations for intersection cohomology of projective varieties. The theorem is proved using weights in ℓ-adic cohomology and the theory of perverse sheaves. A key application is the proof of the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjectures on characters of highest-weight representations of semisimple Lie algebras, via the geometry of Schubert varieties in the flag variety. The intersection cohomology of toric varieties yields the g-theorem for face numbers of simplicial polytopes (Stanley, 1980). For a resolution of singularities π : X̃ → X, the decomposition theorem gives Rπ*ℚX̃[n] ≅ ICX ⊕ (sum of IC complexes on proper subvarieties), so the intersection cohomology of X is a direct summand of the ordinary cohomology of X̃. Examiners frequently ask for the definition of a perverse sheaf, the statement of the decomposition theorem, and its implication for the topology of the Hilbert scheme of points on a surface.

Worked Example: Decomposition Theorem for a Blow-up
Let π : X̃ → X be the blow-up of a smooth complex surface X at a point p, with exceptional divisor E ≅ ℙ1. Compute the decomposition of Rπ*ℚX̃[2] in the derived category of constructible sheaves on X.
Since X̃ is smooth of dimension 2, ℚX̃[2] is a perverse sheaf. The map π is proper and birational. Over X {p}, π is an isomorphism, so the stalk cohomology is ℚ in degree 0. Over p, the fiber is E ≅ ℙ1, with cohomology ℚ in degrees 0 and 2. The decomposition theorem gives Rπ*ℚX̃[2] ≅ ICX ⊕ IC{p}(ℚ)[−1]. Here ICX = ℚX[2] because X is smooth. The summand IC{p}(ℚ)[−1] is the skyscraper sheaf ℚp[−1] (since a point is smooth of dimension 0, its IC complex is the constant sheaf shifted by 0). The shift [−1] accounts for the fact that the cohomology of the fiber E in degree 2 contributes to the stalk in degree 1 of the pushforward. Thus Rπ*ℚX̃[2] ≅ ℚX[2] ⊕ ℚp[−1]. This matches the Leray spectral sequence: H0(X, Rπ*ℚX̃[2]) = H2(X̃, ℚ) = H2(X, ℚ) ⊕ ℚ (the class of E).
Exam Strategy: Intersection Cohomology
Memorize the definition of middle perversity and the fact that ICX = ℚX[n] for smooth X of dimension n. For the decomposition theorem, remember the three key hypotheses: proper map, smooth source, complex algebraic varieties. The conclusion is a direct sum of shifted IC complexes of local systems on strata. A common question asks to identify the summands for a resolution of singularities — the answer always includes ICX plus contributions from the exceptional locus. Know that the hard Lefschetz theorem holds for IH* of projective varieties, and that the Hodge–Riemann relations imply the positivity of intersection pairings on primitive classes.

The Theory of Vertex Operator Algebras and Monstrous Moonshine

A vertex operator algebra (VOA) is an algebraic structure axiomatizing the chiral algebra of a two-dimensional conformal field theory. Formally, a VOA is a ℤ-graded vector space V = ⊕n∈ℤ Vn with a vacuum vector 1 ∈ V0, a conformal vector ω ∈ V2, and a vertex operator map Y : V → (End V)[[z, z−1]] satisfying the vacuum, translation, and locality (Jacobi identity) axioms. The modes of the vertex operators Y(v, z) = ∑n∈ℤ vn z−n−1 generate an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra. The Virasoro algebra, generated by the modes Ln of Y(ω, z), acts on V with central charge c. A VOA is rational if its category of modules is semisimple and finitely generated; it is C2-cofinite if the subspace spanned by v−2w has finite codimension. The Moonshine Module V♮, constructed by Frenkel–Lepowsky–Meurman (1988), is a holomorphic VOA of central charge 24 whose automorphism group is the Monster group M (order ≈ 8×1053). The graded dimension of V♮ is the j-function: j(τ) − 744 = ∑n≥1 dim V♮n qn = q−1 + 196884q + 21493760q2 + ⋯. The Monstrous Moonshine conjectures of Conway–Norton (1979), proven by Borcherds (1992) using the theory of generalized Kac–Moody algebras and the denominator identity of the Monster Lie algebra, state that for each g ∈ M, the McKay–Thompson series Tg(τ) = ∑n≥−1 tr(g | V♮n) qn is a Hauptmodul for a genus-zero subgroup of SL2(ℝ). The proof uses the no-ghost theorem from string theory and the fact that the Monster Lie algebra is a Borcherds–Kac–Moody algebra whose root multiplicities are the coefficients of j. VOAs also classify rational conformal field theories; the Verlinde formula computes fusion rules from the modular S-matrix of characters. Examiners test the axioms of a VOA, the definition of the Virasoro algebra, the statement of the Moonshine conjectures, and the role of the j-function.

The Theory of Floer Homology and the Arnold Conjecture

Floer homology, introduced by Andreas Floer (1988), is an infinite-dimensional Morse theory for the action functional on the loop space of a symplectic manifold. Let (M, ω) be a closed symplectic manifold. For a time-dependent Hamiltonian H : S1 × M → ℝ, the action functional AH on the space of contractible loops ℒM is AH(γ) = −∫D2 ū*ω − ∫01 H(t, γ(t)) dt, where ū : D2 → M extends γ. Its critical points are the 1-periodic orbits of the Hamiltonian vector field XH. The Floer chain complex CF*(H) is the free ℤ2-module generated by non-degenerate 1-periodic orbits, graded by the Conley–Zehnder index. The differential counts solutions u : ℝ × S1 → M of the Floer equation ∂su + J(t, u)(∂tu − XH(t, u)) = 0, asymptotic to orbits at s → ±∞, where J is an ω-compatible almost complex structure. Compactness of the moduli spaces requires ω-tameness and the exclusion of sphere bubbling (e.g., M symplectically aspherical or monotone). The homology HF*(H) is independent of H and J, yielding Hamiltonian Floer homology HF*(M). The Arnold Conjecture (proven by Floer for monotone manifolds, and by Ono, Liu–Tian, Fukaya–Ono for general closed symplectic manifolds) states that the number of 1-periodic orbits of a non-degenerate Hamiltonian is at least the sum of Betti numbers of M. This follows from the isomorphism HF*(M) ≅ H*(M; ℤ2) (PSS isomorphism, Piunikhin–Salamon–Schwarz). For Lagrangian submanifolds L ⊂ M, Lagrangian Floer homology HF*(L, L′) counts intersection points and pseudo-holomorphic strips with boundary on L, L′. The Fukaya category Fuk(M) has objects Lagrangians and morphism spaces HF*(L, L′); its derived category is the target of the Homological Mirror Symmetry conjecture (Kontsevich). Examiners focus on the definition of the Conley–Zehnder index, the Floer equation, the role of monotonicity in preventing bubbling, and the statement of the Arnold conjecture.

The Theory of Condensed Mathematics and Analytic Geometry

Condensed mathematics, developed by Scholze and Clausen (2019), replaces topological spaces with condensed sets — sheaves on the site of profinite sets with the coherent topology — to fix the failure of the category of topological spaces to be cartesian closed. A condensed abelian group is a sheaf of abelian groups on this site; the category Cond(Ab) is an abelian category with all limits and colimits, and a symmetric monoidal structure ⊗ making it a Grothendieck abelian category. The key insight: any topological abelian group G gives a condensed abelian group G♮ by G♮(S) = Cont(S, G) for profinite S. The solid objects are those condensed abelian groups that are derived ℤ-complete and satisfy a homological condition; they form a stable ∞-category Solid equivalent to the derived category of Cond(ℤ)-modules. Analytic geometry in this framework uses condensed rings and analytic rings (condensed rings with a notion of convergent power series). The pro-étale site of a scheme is replaced by the condensed site, and prismatic cohomology (Bhatt–Scholze) becomes the cohomology of the structure sheaf on the condensed site. For a perfectoid space X, the tilt X♭ is a perfectoid space in characteristic p; the tilting equivalence identifies the categories of perfectoid spaces over ℚp and over 𝔽p((t)). The fundamental exact sequence of prismatic cohomology 0 → ΔX → Ainf → OX → 0 relates the prismatic complex ΔX to the Ainf-cohomology. Condensed mathematics also resolves the liquid vector spaces of Scholze: the category of liquid real vector spaces is equivalent to the category of solid ℝ-vector spaces, and the functional analysis of nuclear spaces is recovered internally. Examiners may ask for the definition of a condensed set, the difference between solid and liquid objects, the statement of the tilting equivalence, or the role of the pro-étale site in prismatic cohomology.

  • Confusing the category of motives with the category of pure motives; the former is triangulated (Voevodsky), the latter is conjecturally abelian Tannakian.
  • Assuming the Standard Conjectures are proven; only Conjecture D (numerical = homological equivalence) is a theorem (Jannsen), the rest are open.
  • Treating intersection cohomology as ordinary cohomology of a resolution; IH*(X) is a direct summand of H*(X̃), not the whole thing.
  • Forgetting that the Decomposition Theorem requires a proper map with smooth source; it fails for non-proper or non-smooth maps.
  • Equating vertex operator algebras with chiral algebras; chiral algebras are VOAs on a complex curve with a holomorphicity condition (locality on the formal disk).
  • Believing the Monster group is the automorphism group of the j-function; it is the automorphism group of the Moonshine Module V♮, whose graded dimension is j − 744.
  • Assuming Floer homology is defined for all symplectic manifolds without monotonicity or asphericity; sphere bubbling obstructs compactness in general.
  • Confusing the Conley–Zehnder index with the Morse index; the former is defined for symplectic paths, the latter for critical points of a Morse function.
  • Thinking condensed sets are just topological spaces; they are sheaves on profinite sets, and the embedding of topological spaces is not full.
  • Overlooking that solid objects are a full subcategory of condensed abelian groups, not a quotient; the solidification functor is a left adjoint to the inclusion.

The Theory of Higher Categories and ∞-Categories

Higher category theory extends the classical notion of a category by allowing morphisms between morphisms, and so on, up to any finite level n or infinitely many levels. An (∞,1)-category is a higher category in which all k-morphisms for k > 1 are invertible; it captures the homotopy theory of spaces and spectra. Two principal models dominate modern work: Joyal’s quasicategories (simplicial sets satisfying the inner horn filling condition) and Rezk’s complete Segal spaces (simplicial spaces satisfying a completeness condition). Lurie’s Higher Topos Theory develops the theory of (∞,1)-topoi, showing that the ∞-category of ∞-sheaves on an ∞-site forms an (∞,1)-topos, and that presentable (∞,1)-categories are precisely the localizations of presheaf ∞-categories. The model structure on marked simplicial sets provides a presentation of (∞,1)-categories as fibrant objects, while the theory of (∞,n)-categories (e.g., via Θn-spaces or n-fold complete Segal spaces) allows non‑invertible higher morphisms, essential for extended topological quantum field theories. Key results include the (∞,1)-Yoneda lemma, the adjoint functor theorem for presentable ∞-categories, and the straightening–unstraightening equivalence between Cartesian fibrations and ∞-presheaves. Examiners often test the distinction between strict and weak higher categories, the role of the homotopy coherent nerve, and the fact that the homotopy category of an (∞,1)-category loses higher homotopical information. Applications range from derived algebraic geometry (where the ∞-category of derived stacks replaces the 1‑category of schemes) to factorization homology and the cobordism hypothesis.

The Theory of Homotopy Type Theory and Univalent Foundations

Homotopy type theory (HoTT) interprets Martin‑Löf dependent type theory in the language of ∞‑groupoids: types are spaces, terms are points, identity types are path spaces, and the univalence axiom asserts that equivalence of types coincides with identity. Voevodsky’s simplicial set model (2009) validated univalence, while cubical type theory (Cohen, Coquand, Huber, Mörtberg 2016) gave a constructive computational interpretation with a primitive interval and Kan composition operations. The hierarchy of h‑levels classifies types: h‑level 0 are contractible, 1 are propositions, 2 are sets, 3 are groupoids, etc. Higher inductive types (HITs) allow the definition of spaces by specifying points, paths, and higher paths simultaneously; the circle S¹, the torus, and the truncation operators are canonical examples. The univalence axiom implies function extensionality and the equivalence of categorical and type‑theoretic notions of equivalence. In the cubical setting, the glueing construction provides a direct proof of univalence and yields a canonicity theorem for closed terms of natural number type. Examiners focus on the difference between propositional truncation and set truncation, the computation rules for HITs, and the fact that univalence is inconsistent with proof‑irrelevant classical logic unless one works in a predicative universe hierarchy. The synthetic approach to homotopy theory in HoTT has produced machine‑checked proofs of the Freudenthal suspension theorem, the Blakers–Massey theorem, and the calculation of π₄(S³) = ℤ/2.

Worked Example: Distinguishing (∞,1)-Categories from (∞,2)-Categories
Explain why the ∞-category of (∞,1)-categories is itself an (∞,2)-category, and why the homotopy 2‑category of this (∞,2)-category is not equivalent to the 1‑category of (∞,1)-categories up to equivalence.
An (∞,1)-category has invertible k‑morphisms for k>1. The collection of all (∞,1)-categories forms an (∞,2)-category because functors between (∞,1)-categories can be composed strictly, but natural transformations between functors are only invertible up to higher homotopies (modifications). Thus we have non‑invertible 2‑morphisms (natural transformations) and invertible 3‑morphisms (modifications). The homotopy 2‑category discards all invertible 3‑morphisms and above, retaining only the 2‑morphisms up to isomorphism. However, two (∞,1)-categories can be equivalent via a functor that is not an isomorphism on the nose; such equivalences become isomorphisms in the homotopy 2‑category only after passing to the homotopy category of the (∞,2)-category, which identifies functors that are connected by a zig‑zag of natural equivalences. The 1‑category of (∞,1)-categories up to equivalence collapses all natural transformations to identities, losing the 2‑categorical structure entirely. Hence the homotopy 2‑category retains non‑trivial 2‑morphisms (e.g., the automorphism 2‑group of the identity functor), while the 1‑category does not.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a comparison of higher categorical models, first state the universal property each model satisfies (e.g., quasicategories model (∞,1)-categories via the Joyal model structure). Then note the specific technical advantage: quasicategories have a simple nerve functor, complete Segal spaces have a built‑in completeness condition, and Θn-spaces model (∞,n)-categories. Cite the key equivalence theorems (Joyal–Tierney, Rezk, Barwick–Schommer‑Pries) to show you know the landscape.

The Theory of Quantum Groups and Hopf Algebras

Quantum groups are non‑commutative, non‑cocommutative Hopf algebras that deform the universal enveloping algebra U(𝔤) of a semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤. Drinfeld and Jimbo independently introduced the quantized enveloping algebra Uq(𝔤) in 1985, depending on a parameter q (generic or a root of unity). As a Hopf algebra, Uq(𝔤) possesses a coproduct Δ, counit ε, and antipode S satisfying the usual axioms; the R‑matrix R ∈ Uq(𝔤) ⊗ Uq(𝔤) solves the quantum Yang–Baxter equation and implements braiding in the category of finite‑dimensional representations. At generic q, the representation theory mirrors the classical case: highest‑weight modules are classified by dominant integral weights, and the tensor product decomposes via the same Clebsch–Gordan rules. At roots of unity, the representation category becomes non‑semisimple, giving rise to modular tensor categories that underlie topological quantum field theories and invariants of 3‑manifolds (Reshetikhin–Turaev). The dual Hopf algebra, the quantum coordinate ring Oq(G), provides a deformation of the algebra of regular functions on the corresponding algebraic group G. Lusztig’s canonical basis and Kashiwara’s crystal bases give combinatorial models for representations at q = 0, leading to the theory of crystal graphs and the proof of the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjectures for quantum groups. Quantum affine algebras Uq(ĝ) and the associated Yangians extend the construction to infinite‑dimensional settings, producing solutions of the Yang–Baxter equation with spectral parameter and the algebraic Bethe ansatz. Examiners test the definition of a Hopf algebra, the construction of the R‑matrix for sl₂, the distinction between the Drinfeld–Jimbo and FRT presentations, and the role of the quantum determinant in defining quantum SLn.

The Theory of Arithmetic Geometry: Shimura Varieties and the Langlands Correspondence

Shimura varieties are higher‑dimensional analogues of modular curves, defined as moduli spaces of abelian varieties with additional structure (polarizations, endomorphisms, level structures) that admit a canonical model over a number field (the reflex field). The simplest case is the modular curve Y(N) = Γ(N)\ℌ, parametrizing elliptic curves with full level‑N structure. For a reductive group G over ℚ and a Hermitian symmetric domain X, the Shimura variety ShK(G,X) = G(ℚ)X × G(𝔸f)/K carries an action of the absolute Galois group Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ) and of the Hecke algebra. The Langlands correspondence predicts a bijection between automorphic representations of G(𝔸) and Galois representations into the L‑group LG. For GL(2), the Eichler–Shimura construction attaches a 2‑dimensional ℓ‑adic Galois representation to a cuspidal eigenform, realizing the local Langlands correspondence at unramified places via the Satake isomorphism. The work of Harris–Taylor (2001) and Henniart (2000) established the local Langlands correspondence for GL(n) over p‑adic fields using the geometry of Lubin–Tate towers and the Harris–Taylor method of comparing trace formulas. The global Langlands correspondence for GL(n) over number fields was completed by Arthur (2013) using the stabilized trace formula and endoscopic classification. Shimura varieties provide the geometric setting for the construction of Galois representations attached to automorphic forms (Kuga–Sato varieties, étale cohomology of Shimura varieties). The recent proof of the local Langlands correspondence for inner forms of GL(n) by Kaletha and the development of the categorical Langlands program (geometric Langlands for curves over ℂ, using D‑modules on BunG) extend the picture. Examiners focus on the definition of a Shimura datum (G,X), the reflex field, the canonical model theorem of Shimura–Deligne, the action of Hecke operators on cohomology, and the statement of the local and global Langlands conjectures for GL(n).

The Theory of Spectral Sequences and Their Applications

A spectral sequence is a computational tool that organizes a sequence of successive approximations to the homology or cohomology of a filtered complex. Formally, it consists of a family of bigraded modules Erp,q with differentials dr of bidegree (r, 1−r) such that Er+1 = H(Er, dr). The spectral sequence converges to the associated graded of the target object if the filtration is exhaustive and Hausdorff. The Serre spectral sequence arises from a fibration F → E → B: E2p,q = Hp(B; Hq(F)) ⇒ Hp+q(E). The Leray spectral sequence computes sheaf cohomology via a composition of functors: E2p,q = Hp(X, Rqf*ℱ) ⇒ Hp+q(Y, ℱ). The Adams spectral sequence, built from the stable homotopy category and a ring spectrum E, has E2s,t = Exts,tE*E(E*, E*) converging to the E‑nilpotent completion of the stable homotopy groups of spheres. The Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence computes generalized cohomology theories from ordinary cohomology. In group cohomology, the Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence for a group extension 1 → N → G → Q → 1 has E2p,q = Hp(Q, Hq(N, M)) ⇒ Hp+q(G, M). Key techniques include identifying differentials via edge homomorphisms, transgression, and the use of multiplicative structures (cup products) to propagate information. Examiners test the ability to set up the Serre spectral sequence for a given fibration, to compute low‑degree differentials using the transgression, and to recognize when a spectral sequence collapses at E2 (e.g., for a trivial fibration or when the base is a sphere). The Adams spectral sequence is a standard tool for calculating π*(S) at a prime; the first non‑trivial differential d2(h0) = h1² in the classical Adams spectral sequence at p=2 illustrates the interplay between algebraic Ext groups and topological information.

  • Confusing the convergence of a spectral sequence with the collapse at a finite page; convergence only guarantees an associated graded isomorphism, not that all differentials vanish.
  • Assuming the E2 page of the Serre spectral sequence is always Hp(B; Hq(F)) without checking local coefficient systems; monodromy can twist the coefficients.
  • Treating the univalence axiom as a mere propositional extensionality principle; univalence equates equivalence of types with identity, which is strictly stronger.
  • Believing that quantum groups at roots of unity are semisimple; the representation category becomes a modular tensor category with non‑semisimple projective covers.
  • Overlooking that Shimura varieties require a Hermitian symmetric domain; not every reductive group yields a Shimura variety (e.g., split groups of higher rank without a suitable Hodge structure).
  • Thinking the Adams spectral sequence converges to the actual stable homotopy groups of spheres; it converges to the E‑nilpotent completion, which may differ from the true groups if E‑localization loses information.
  • Equating the homotopy 2‑category of an (∞,2)-category with the 1‑category of its objects up to equivalence; the former retains non‑invertible 2‑morphisms that the latter discards.

The sections above provide a rigorous foundation for the advanced topics that frequently appear in competitive mathematics examinations.

The Theory of Hodge Structures and Period Domains

A pure Hodge structure of weight k on a finite‑dimensional ℚ‑vector space V is a decomposition V⊗ℂ = ⊕p+q=k Vp,q with Vq,p = Vp,q. The Hodge filtration Fp = ⊕r≥p Vr,k−r determines the decomposition. For a smooth projective variety X over ℂ, the cohomology Hk(X, ℚ) carries a canonical pure Hodge structure (Hodge theory). The period domain D parametrizes all Hodge structures of given Hodge numbers on a fixed lattice with a polarization; it is a homogeneous space Gℝ/H where G is the real Mumford–Tate group and H a compact subgroup. The period map sends a family of varieties to D and satisfies Griffiths transversality: the differential maps the tangent space into ⊕p Hom(Fp/Fp+1, Fp−1/Fp). Mixed Hodge structures, introduced by Deligne, extend the theory to singular or non‑compact varieties; they carry a weight filtration W and a Hodge filtration F such that the graded pieces are pure Hodge structures. The limiting mixed Hodge structure of a degenerating family encodes monodromy via the nilpotent orbit theorem (Schmid). Examiners often test the definition of a polarized Hodge structure, the description of the period domain for weight‑1 (Siegel upper half‑space) and weight‑2 (type IV domains), and the statement of the global Torelli theorem for K3 surfaces. A typical trap is to confuse the Hodge filtration with the weight filtration; they are independent in mixed Hodge theory.

The Theory of Derived Categories and Fourier–Mukai Transforms

The bounded derived category Db(Coh(X)) of coherent sheaves on a smooth projective variety X is a triangulated category with shift functor [1] and distinguished triangles coming from short exact sequences. A Fourier–Mukai transform is an exact functor Φℰ: Db(Coh(X)) → Db(Coh(Y)) given by Φℰ(−) = RπY*(πX*(−) ⊗L ℰ), where ℰ ∈ Db(Coh(X×Y)) is the kernel and πX, πY are projections. Orlov’s representability theorem states that any exact equivalence between derived categories of smooth projective varieties is of Fourier–Mukai type. For an abelian variety A with dual Â, the Poincaré line bundle ℙ on A×Â yields the classical Fourier–Mukai equivalence. On K3 surfaces, derived equivalences are classified by Mukai: they correspond to Hodge isometries of the Mukai lattice H*(X, ℤ) preserving the orientation of positive planes. Bridgeland stability conditions on Db(Coh(X)) form a complex manifold; wall‑crossing describes how the set of stable objects changes. Examiners focus on the definition of the convolution product, the adjoint pair (Φℰ, ΦℰR), and the criterion for an equivalence: the kernel must induce an isomorphism on Hochschild homology and the Fourier–Mukai partners must have isomorphic canonical bundles. A common error is to assume every autoequivalence of Db(Coh(X)) comes from a geometric automorphism; on K3 surfaces there are many non‑geometric autoequivalences (spherical twists).

Fourier–Mukai Equivalence on an Abelian Variety
Show that the Fourier–Mukai transform with kernel the Poincaré line bundle ℙ on A×Â gives an equivalence between Db(Coh(A)) and Db(Coh(Â)).
Let πA, πÂ be the projections. Define Φℙ(ℰ) = RπÂ*(πA*ℰ ⊗ ℙ). The dual kernel is ℙ∨ on Â×A (up to shift). By the theorem of Mukai, the composition Φℙ∨ ∘ Φℙ is isomorphic to (−1)A*[−g] where g = dim A. Since (−1)A is an automorphism, Φℙ is an equivalence with quasi‑inverse Φℙ∨[g]. The key steps: (1) compute the convolution kernel ℙ ⋆ ℙ∨ using the seesaw principle; (2) identify it with the structure sheaf of the diagonal shifted by −g; (3) invoke the criterion that a Fourier–Mukai functor is an equivalence iff its kernel induces an isomorphism on Hochschild homology, which holds because ℙ is a universal family of degree‑zero line bundles.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks to verify a Fourier–Mukai equivalence, first write down the kernel and its dual. Check that the convolution kernel is the diagonal sheaf (up to shift) using base‑change and the projection formula. If the variety is an abelian variety, recall the standard Poincaré bundle and the shift by the dimension. For K3 surfaces, remember that any Hodge isometry of the Mukai lattice lifts to an autoequivalence; cite Orlov’s theorem.

The Theory of Geometric Invariant Theory and Moduli Spaces

Geometric Invariant Theory (GIT), developed by Mumford, constructs quotients of algebraic varieties by reductive group actions in the category of schemes. Given a linearized action of a reductive group G on a projective variety X with an ample line bundle L, a point x ∈ X is semistable if some G‑invariant section of L⊗n does not vanish at x; it is stable if its orbit is closed in the semistable locus and its stabilizer is finite. The GIT quotient X//G = Proj(⊕n≥0 H⁰(X, L⊗n)G) parametrizes closed orbits in the semistable locus. The Hilbert–Mumford numerical criterion reduces (semi)stability to one‑parameter subgroups: x is semistable iff for every λ: 𝔾m → G, the weight μ(x, λ) ≥ 0. Variation of GIT (VGIT) studies how the quotient changes as the linearization varies; walls in the ample cone correspond to strictly semistable loci, and crossing a wall yields a birational transformation (flip or flop). Applications include the moduli space Mg of stable curves (Deligne–Mumford), the moduli of vector bundles on a curve (Narasimhan–Seshadri, Gieseker–Maruyama), and the moduli of sheaves on surfaces (Mukai). The Kempf–Ness theorem identifies the GIT quotient with a symplectic quotient in the Kähler setting. Examiners test the definition of (semi)stability for vector bundles (slope stability μ(E) = deg(E)/rk(E)), the construction of the Quot scheme, and the fact that the moduli space of stable bundles is a projective variety. A frequent trap is to confuse GIT stability with slope stability; they coincide for vector bundles on curves via the Narasimhan–Seshadri correspondence but differ in higher dimension.

The Theory of Symplectic Topology and Hamiltonian Floer Homology

Symplectic topology studies manifolds (M, ω) with a closed non‑degenerate 2‑form ω. Hamiltonian dynamics are generated by a time‑dependent Hamiltonian H: S¹×M → ℝ; its flow φt preserves ω. The Arnold conjecture asserts that a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism has at least as many fixed points as the sum of Betti numbers of M. Floer homology provides a Morse‑theoretic proof: for a non‑degenerate Hamiltonian, the chain complex CF*(H) is generated by 1‑periodic orbits, graded by the Conley–Zehnder index. The differential counts solutions of Floer’s equation ∂su + J(∂tu − XH(u)) = 0 on the cylinder ℝ×S¹, where J is an ω‑compatible almost complex structure. The resulting homology HF*(H) is independent of H and J and isomorphic to the singular homology of M (Piunikhin–Salamon–Schwarz isomorphism). Spectral invariants c(α, H) associate to each quantum homology class α a real number measuring the minimal action of a cycle representing α; they satisfy the triangle inequality and give rise to the Hofer metric on the Hamiltonian group. Gromov–Witten invariants count pseudoholomorphic curves and define quantum cohomology QH*(M), a deformation of the cup product. The Fukaya category, an A∞‑category of Lagrangian submanifolds, categorifies Floer homology. Examiners focus on the definition of the Conley–Zehnder index, the compactness theorem for Floer trajectories (Gromov compactness), and the isomorphism HF ≅ H*(M). A common mistake is to assume Floer homology is defined for all symplectic manifolds; monotonicity or exactness conditions are required to avoid bubbling of holomorphic spheres.

The Theory of Tropical Geometry and Degenerations

Tropical geometry replaces the usual arithmetic (ℝ, +, ×) with the tropical semiring (ℝ ∪ {−∞}, ⊕, ⊙) where a ⊕ b = max(a, b) and a ⊙ b = a + b. A tropical polynomial is a piecewise‑linear convex function; its tropical hypersurface is the corner locus where the maximum is attained at least twice. Tropical varieties are balanced polyhedral complexes of pure dimension, satisfying the zero‑tension condition at each codimension‑1 cell. The fundamental theorem of tropical geometry (Kapranov, Sturmfels) states that the tropicalization of an algebraic variety over a valued field (e.g., Puiseux series) coincides with the set of valuations of its points. Degenerations of algebraic varieties to toric varieties are captured by the extended tropicalization map; the central fiber of a toric degeneration is a union of toric varieties glued along toric strata, dual to a subdivision of the Newton polytope. Mikhalkin’s correspondence theorem equates genus‑0 Gromov–Witten invariants of toric surfaces with counts of tropical curves of given degree and incidence conditions. Tropical methods compute enumerative invariants (e.g., Hurwitz numbers, Welschinger invariants) and provide combinatorial models for mirror symmetry (Gross–Siebert program). Examiners test the definition of the tropical semiring, the balancing condition, the tropicalization of a hypersurface defined by a Laurent polynomial, and the statement of the correspondence theorem for plane curves. A typical trap is to treat tropical addition as ordinary addition; the idempotent nature (a ⊕ a = a) is essential for the geometry.

  • Confusing the Hodge filtration with the weight filtration in mixed Hodge structures; they are independent and serve different purposes.
  • Assuming every derived autoequivalence of a K3 surface is induced by a geometric automorphism; spherical twists provide counterexamples.
  • Mixing up GIT stability with slope stability for sheaves on higher‑dimensional varieties; they coincide only on curves.
  • Believing Floer homology is defined for arbitrary symplectic manifolds without monotonicity or exactness hypotheses; sphere bubbling obstructs the differential.
  • Treating tropical addition as ordinary addition and forgetting the idempotent property a ⊕ a = a, which underlies the balancing condition.
  • Overlooking that the period map for weight‑1 Hodge structures lands in the Siegel upper half‑space, while weight‑2 lands in a type IV domain; the domains are not isomorphic.
  • Thinking the Fourier–Mukai kernel must be a sheaf; it can be any object in the derived category of the product.

The Theory of Prismatic Cohomology and the Hodge‑Tate Comparison

Prismatic cohomology, introduced by Bhatt and Scholze, provides a unified framework for p‑adic cohomology theories such as crystalline, de Rham, and étale cohomology. A prism is a pair (A, I) where A is a δ‑ring (a ring equipped with a Frobenius lift δ) and I ⊂ A is an ideal such that A is (p, I)‑complete, p ∈ I + φ(I)A, and the Frobenius φ on A satisfies φ(x) ≡ x^p (mod p). The key example is the Breuil‑Kisin prism (A_inf, (ξ)) for a perfectoid field, where A_inf = W(O_C^♭) and ξ generates the kernel of the Fontaine map θ: A_inf → O_C.

The prismatic site (X)_△ of a p‑adic formal scheme X consists of prisms (A, I) equipped with a map Spf(A/I) → X. The structure sheaf O_△ assigns to each prism its ring A. Prismatic cohomology RΓ_△(X) = RΓ((X)_△, O_△) is a derived complete complex of A‑modules. The Hodge‑Tate comparison states that for a smooth proper formal scheme X over O_K, there is a canonical isomorphism H^i_△(X) ⊗^L_A A/I ≅ ⊕_j Hi‑j(X, Ω^jX/O_K)[‑j] in the derived category of A/I‑modules. This recovers the Hodge‑Tate decomposition of p‑adic étale cohomology after base change to C.

The prismatic comparison theorem identifies RΓ_△(X) ⊗^L_A A_inf with the A_inf‑cohomology of the associated perfectoid space, and after further base change to B_dR+ recovers de Rham cohomology. The Nygaard filtration on prismatic cohomology, defined by the divided powers of I, plays the role of the Hodge filtration. Examiners often test the definition of a prism, the construction of the prismatic site, and the statement of the Hodge‑Tate comparison. A common trap is to confuse the Nygaard filtration with the Hodge filtration; they coincide only after suitable base change and completion.

The Theory of Motivic Homotopy Theory and the Morel‑Voevodsky Category

Motivic homotopy theory, developed by Morel and Voevodsky, constructs a homotopy category of schemes that mimics classical topological homotopy theory. The starting point is the category Sm_k of smooth schemes over a field k. One inverts the Nisnevich local weak equivalences and the A1‑homotopy equivalences (projection X × A1 → X). The resulting A1‑homotopy category H(k) is a symmetric monoidal triangulated category. Its spheres are the Tate objects Sp,q = (S1)∧p ∧ (G_m)∧q, where G_m = A1 {0}.

Representable motivic spectra are built from suspension spectra Σ^∞_T X_+ with T = A1/(A1 {0}) ≅ S2,1. The motivic stable homotopy category SH(k) is obtained by stabilizing H(k) with respect to T. Voevodsky’s construction of motivic cohomology uses the complex of sheaves Z(q) = C_* (Z_tr (G_m∧q))[‑q] in the Nisnevich topology. The motivic cohomology groups Hp,q(X, Z) = HomSH(k)(Σ^∞_T X_+, Z(q)[p]) satisfy the expected properties: homotopy invariance, Nisnevich excision, and a projective bundle formula.

The Morel‑Voevodsky theorem identifies the motivic cohomology of a point with Milnor K‑theory: Hq,q(Spec k, Z) ≅ K^M_q(k). The Bloch‑Kato conjecture (now the norm residue isomorphism theorem, proved by Voevodsky, Rost, and others) asserts that the Galois symbol K^M_q(k)/ℓ → H^qét(k, μ_ℓ⊗q) is an isomorphism for ℓ invertible in k. This is a deep consequence of the motivic machinery. Examiners focus on the definition of the A1‑localization, the role of the Nisnevich topology, and the computation of motivic cohomology of fields. A frequent mistake is to treat the Tate sphere T as the ordinary topological sphere S2; the weight grading q is essential for the Adams‑Novikov spectral sequence in motivic homotopy theory.

Worked Example: Prismatic Cohomology of Z_p
Compute the prismatic cohomology RΓ_△(Z_p) for the Breuil‑Kisin prism (A_inf, (ξ)) with A_inf = W(F_p[[u1/p^∞]]) and ξ = [u]‑p.
For X = Spf Z_p, the prismatic site has a final object given by the prism (A_inf, (ξ)) itself. The structure sheaf evaluates to A_inf. Since the site is contractible, RΓ_△(Z_p) ≅ A_inf derived (p, ξ)‑complete. The Hodge‑Tate comparison gives H0_△ ⊗ A_inf/(ξ) ≅ Z_p and higher cohomology vanishes. Thus RΓ_△(Z_p) is quasi‑isomorphic to A_inf placed in degree 0.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a comparison between prismatic and crystalline cohomology, first write down the prism (A, I) and the crystalline site. Then state the base‑change isomorphisms: RΓ_△ ⊗^L_A A/I ≅ RΓ_crys ⊗^LW(k) A/I. Remember that the Nygaard filtration on the prismatic side corresponds to the Hodge filtration on the crystalline side after dividing by p. This two‑step translation is the core of most examiner‑level problems.

The Theory of Higher Categorical Structures in Topological Quantum Field Theory

The cobordism hypothesis, proved by Lurie, classifies fully extended topological quantum field theories (TQFTs) as symmetric monoidal functors Z: Bord_nfr → C, where Bord_nfr is the (∞,n)‑category of framed n‑dimensional cobordisms and C is a symmetric monoidal (∞,n)‑category. The hypothesis asserts that such functors are equivalent to fully dualizable objects in C. For n = 2, a 2‑dimensional TQFT corresponds to a Calabi‑Yau object (a Frobenius algebra) in C; for n = 3, it corresponds to a modular tensor category.

The (∞,n)‑category Bord_nfr is generated by the point with its framing. Its morphisms are built from handlebodies, and the symmetric monoidal structure is disjoint union. The fully dualizable condition means that the object has duals at every level up to n, and all evaluation and coevaluation maps admit adjoints. In the case C = Vect_k (the (∞,1)‑category of chain complexes), fully dualizable objects are precisely finite‑dimensional vector spaces, recovering the classical Atiyah‑Segal axioms.

The Theory of Adeles, Ideles, and the Adelic Formulation of Automorphic Forms

The adele ring Aℚ of the rational numbers is the restricted product of the completions ℚp over all primes p (including the archimedean completion ℝ) with respect to the subrings ℤp. An adele is a sequence (a∞, a2, a3, a5, …) where ap ∈ ℚp and ap ∈ ℤp for all but finitely many p. The idele group Iℚ is the group of units of Aℚ, consisting of adeles with all components non-zero and almost all components in ℤp×. The topology on Aℚ is the restricted product topology, making it a locally compact ring; ℚ embeds diagonally as a discrete cocompact subring. The quotient Aℚ/ℚ is compact, a fact equivalent to the finiteness of the class number and the Dirichlet unit theorem. Automorphic forms are functions on the adelic quotient G(ℚ)G(Aℚ) for a reductive algebraic group G, satisfying invariance under a maximal compact subgroup Kf ⊂ G(Af), moderate growth, and eigenfunction conditions for the center of the universal enveloping algebra of the Lie algebra of G(ℝ). The adelic formulation unifies classical modular forms (G = GL2) and Maass forms, and makes the action of Hecke operators transparent: they arise from double cosets KfgKf in G(Af). The Langlands correspondence predicts a bijection between irreducible admissible representations of G(Aℚ) occurring in L2(G(ℚ)G(Aℚ)) and Langlands parameters, which are homomorphisms from the conjectural Langlands group Lℚ to the L-group LG. The constant term of an automorphic form along a parabolic subgroup P = MN is defined by integration over N(ℚ)N(Aℚ), and cuspidal automorphic forms are those with vanishing constant terms for all proper parabolics. The spectral decomposition of L2(G(ℚ)G(Aℚ)) into cuspidal, residual, and continuous spectra is the adelic analogue of the classical spectral theory of the Laplacian on modular curves. Examiners test the definition of the restricted product, the compactness of Aℚ/ℚ, the definition of automorphic forms via moderate growth and K-finiteness, and the relation between classical Hecke operators and adelic double cosets.

The Theory of Quantum Cohomology, Gromov-Witten Invariants, and Mirror Symmetry

Quantum cohomology deforms the ordinary cup product on the cohomology ring H*(X, ℚ) of a symplectic manifold (or smooth projective variety) X by incorporating counts of pseudoholomorphic curves. For classes α, β, γ ∈ H*(X), the quantum product α ⋆ β is defined by ⟨α ⋆ β, γ⟩ = Σd ∈ H2(X,ℤ) ⟨α, β, γ⟩0,3,d qd, where ⟨α, β, γ⟩0,3,d is the genus-zero three-point Gromov-Witten invariant counting stable maps f: ℙ1 → X of degree d with three marked points mapping to cycles Poincaré dual to α, β, γ, and qd are formal variables in the Novikov ring. The associativity of ⋆ is equivalent to the WDVV (Witten-Dijkgraaf-Verlinde-Verlinde) equations, a system of quadratic relations among the Gromov-Witten invariants. For X = ℙn, the quantum cohomology ring is ℚ[H, q]/(Hn+1 = q), where H is the hyperplane class. Mirror symmetry predicts an isomorphism between the quantum cohomology of a Calabi-Yau threefold X and the variation of Hodge structure of its mirror Y, identifying the quantum product with the Yukawa coupling on the complex moduli space of Y. The A-model topological string computes Gromov-Witten invariants; the B-model computes periods of the holomorphic three-form on Y. The genus-zero mirror theorem (Givental, Lian-Liu-Yau) proves this for toric complete intersections. Higher-genus invariants are organized by the holomorphic anomaly equations (Bershadsky-Cecotti-Ooguri-Vafa). Examiners focus on the definition of stable maps and the moduli space M0,n(X, d), the virtual fundamental class, the divisor and fundamental class axioms for Gromov-Witten invariants, the WDVV equations, and the statement of the mirror conjecture for the quintic threefold.

Worked Computation: Quantum Product on ℙ2
Compute the quantum product H ⋆ H in QH*(ℙ2), where H ∈ H2(ℙ2) is the hyperplane class, and verify associativity for H ⋆ H ⋆ H.
The classical cohomology ring is H*(ℙ2) = ℚ[H]/(H3 = 0). The quantum product is defined by ⟨H ⋆ H, H⟩ = Σd≥0 ⟨H, H, H⟩0,3,d qd. The only non-zero genus-zero three-point invariant is ⟨H, H, H⟩0,3,1 = 1 (one line through two points in ℙ2). Thus ⟨H ⋆ H, H⟩ = q, so H ⋆ H = q · 1 (since H is dual to itself under Poincaré pairing). Then H ⋆ H ⋆ H = (H ⋆ H) ⋆ H = q · H. On the other hand, H ⋆ (H ⋆ H) = H ⋆ (q · 1) = q · H. Associativity holds. The quantum cohomology ring is ℚ[H, q]/(H3 = q).
Exam Strategy: Gromov-Witten Axioms
When a question asks to compute a Gromov-Witten invariant, first check the dimension constraint: the virtual dimension of M0,n(X, d) is dim X + ∫d c1(TX) + n - 3. The invariant vanishes unless the sum of codimensions of the insertions equals this virtual dimension. Use the divisor axiom ⟨τ0(D) ∏ τki(γi)⟩0,n,d = (∫d D) ⟨∏ τki(γi)⟩0,n,d + Σ ⟨τki-1(D·γi) ∏j≠i τkj(γj)⟩0,n,d to reduce insertions of divisor classes. The fundamental class axiom removes a marked point with insertion 1. These axioms reduce computations to a finite set of primary invariants.

The Theory of p-adic Differential Equations and the p-adic Local Langlands Correspondence

A p-adic differential equation on a rigid analytic space X over ℚp is a finite free 𝒪X-module ℰ equipped with an integrable connection ∇: ℰ → ℰ ⊗ Ω1X. The Robba ring ℛ is the ring of germs of analytic functions on an open annulus {z : 0 < |z| < 1} around the boundary of the open unit disc; it is the p-adic analogue of the field of formal Laurent series. A (φ, Γ)-module over ℛ is a finite free ℛ-module D equipped with a semilinear Frobenius φ and a continuous semilinear action of Γ = Gal(ℚp(μp∞)/ℚp) ≅ ℤp×, commuting with φ. Fontaine's equivalence of categories states that the category of p-adic Galois representations of Gℚp on finite-dimensional ℚp-vector spaces is equivalent to the category of étale (φ, Γ)-modules over ℛ. The p-adic local Langlands correspondence for GL2(ℚp) (Colmez, Berger-Breuil, Kisin) establishes a bijection between irreducible admissible unitary Banach space representations of GL2(ℚp) over ℚp and two-dimensional p-adic Galois representations of Gℚp. The correspondence is realized via the functor Dpst (potentially semistable Dieudonné module) and the (φ, Γ)-module Drig†(V) of Berger. For a de Rham representation V, the locally analytic vectors in the corresponding Banach representation Π(V) are described by the locally analytic socle, which is a direct sum of principal series representations determined by the Hodge-Tate weights of V. The Breuil-Schneider conjecture (proved by Colmez for GL2) predicts the locally analytic socle for general reductive groups. Examiners test the definition of the Robba ring, the equivalence between Galois representations and (φ, Γ)-modules, the classification of trianguline representations, the statement of the p-adic local Langlands correspondence for GL2, and the relation between Hodge-Tate weights and the locally analytic socle.

The Theory of Higher Topos Theory, ∞-Topoi, and Descent

An ∞-topos is an ∞-category that satisfies the higher-categorical analogues of Giraud's axioms: it has all small colimits, colimits are universal (preserved by pullback), coproducts are disjoint, every groupoid object is effective, and there exists a small set of generators. Equivalently, an ∞-topos is a left exact localization of an ∞-category of presheaves of spaces PSh∞(𝒞) = Fun(𝒞op, 𝒮) on a small ∞-category 𝒞. The ∞-category of sheaves of spaces Shv∞(𝒞, τ) on an ∞-site (𝒞, τ) is an ∞-topos. The fundamental theorem of higher topos theory (Lurie) states that every ∞-topos is equivalent to Shv∞(𝒞, τ) for some ∞-site. Descent in an ∞-topos is the statement that for any covering sieve R → y(c) in 𝒞, the limit of the Čech nerve of the cover computes the value of a sheaf on c. The ∞-category of ∞-topoi and geometric morphisms forms an ∞-category Topos∞. A geometric morphism f: ℰ → ℱ is an adjunction (f* ⊣ f*) with f* left exact. The ∞-topos of spaces 𝒮 is the terminal object. The shape of an ∞-topos ℰ is the pro-space Shape(ℰ) = limX∈ℰ X, classifying locally constant ∞-stacks on ℰ. Cohomology in an ∞-topos is defined by Hn(ℰ; A) = π-n Mapℰ(1, A) for a spectrum object A ∈ Sp(ℰ). The Postnikov tower of an object X ∈ ℰ gives a filtration by n-truncated objects, and the k-invariants live in cohomology groups. The ∞-topos of condensed sets (Scholze) is the ∞-category of sheaves of sets on the site of profinite sets with the coherent topology; it behaves like the ∞-category of topological spaces but with better formal properties for functional analysis. Examiners focus on the definition of an ∞-topos via Giraud's axioms, the equivalence with sheaves on an ∞-site, the characterization of geometric morphisms, the computation of shape for the étale ∞-topos of a scheme, and the difference between hypercompleteness and non-hypercompleteness (e.g., the ∞-topos of sheaves on a non-Noetherian scheme).

The Theory of Geometric Langlands Correspondence and D-modules

The geometric Langlands correspondence, formulated by Drinfeld and Lafforgue for function fields and extended by Beilinson-Drinfeld and Gaitsgory to the categorical level, is a geometric analogue of the classical Langlands correspondence for a reductive group G over a smooth projective curve X over an algebraically closed field k. The automorphic side is the derived category of D-modules on the moduli stack BunG of G-bundles on X, denoted D-mod(BunG). The spectral side is the derived category of quasi-coherent sheaves on the moduli stack LocSysLG of LG-local systems (flat LG-bundles) on X, denoted QCoh(LocSysLG). The conjecture asserts an equivalence of symmetric monoidal ∞-categories D-mod(BunG) ≃ QCoh(LocSysLG) compatible with Hecke operators. Hecke operators are correspondences Heckex ⊂ BunG × BunG parametrizing modifications of G-bundles at a point x ∈ X; they act on D-mod(BunG) by convolution. Under the equivalence, the Hecke operator at x corresponds to tensoring with the fiber functor at x on LocSysLG. The Whittaker category Whitt(G) is the full subcategory of D-mod(BunG) consisting of objects with a Whittaker model; the geometric Langlands equivalence restricts to an equivalence Whitt(G) ≃ QCoh(LocSysLG). The proof for GLn (Gaitsgory, Raskin, and others) uses the theory of ind-coherent sheaves, the categorical trace, and the spectral decomposition of the Hecke category. The geometric Satake equivalence identifies the spherical Hecke category with Rep(LG). The categorical Langlands correspondence for the curve X = ℙ1 with tame ramification is equivalent to the Kazhdan-Lusztig equivalence between representations of the affine Lie algebra at critical level and D-modules on the affine Grassmannian. Examiners test the definition of the moduli stacks BunG and LocSysLG, the action of Hecke operators, the statement of the categorical equivalence, the role of the Whittaker normalization, and the geometric Satake equivalence.

  • Confusing the adele ring (a ring) with the idele group (its unit group); the restricted product topology on the ideles is NOT the subspace topology from the adeles.
  • Assuming all Gromov-Witten invariants are enumerative; they are virtual counts defined via the virtual fundamental class, and can be negative or rational.
  • Treating the Robba ring as a field; it is a Bézout domain but not a field, and its units are series with non-zero constant term.
  • Believing every ∞-topos is hypercomplete; the ∞-topos of sheaves on a non-Noetherian scheme is typically not hypercomplete, and the hypercompletion map is not an equivalence.
  • Confusing the geometric Langlands correspondence for D-modules with the classical Langlands correspondence for automorphic forms; the former is a categorical equivalence of derived categories, the latter is a bijection of irreducible representations.
  • Neglecting the monoidal structure in the geometric Langlands equivalence; the compatibility with Hecke operators (convolution on the automorphic side, tensor product on the spectral side) is essential.
  • Assuming the p-adic local Langlands correspondence holds for all reductive groups; it is only fully established for GL2(ℚp) and partially for GLn(ℚp).

The Theory of Derived Deformation Theory and the Cotangent Complex

Derived deformation theory extends classical deformation theory by replacing the tangent‑obstruction complex with the cotangent complex LX of a scheme or stack X. The cotangent complex was constructed by Illusie in the early 1970s building on Quillen’s model‑category approach to homotopical algebra. For a morphism f: X → Y of derived schemes, the relative cotangent complex LX/Y controls infinitesimal deformations: the space of first‑order deformations is Ext0(LX/Y, M) and obstructions lie in Ext1(LX/Y, M) for a quasi‑coherent module M. When X is a local complete intersection, LX is perfect of amplitude [−1,0] and recovers the classical conormal sequence. In derived algebraic geometry the cotangent complex becomes a fundamental object: it represents the functor of derivations on the ∞‑category of derived rings, and its formation commutes with arbitrary base change. This functoriality underpins the construction of virtual fundamental classes on moduli stacks such as Mg,n and the definition of Gromov–Witten invariants via the perfect obstruction theory of Behrend–Fantechi.

A key computational tool is the transitivity triangle LY/Z ⊗ OX → LX/Z → LX/Y → for composable morphisms X → Y → Z. In practice one often computes LX by presenting X as a derived quotient of a smooth algebra by a regular sequence; the resulting two‑term complex is the derived analogue of the Jacobian matrix. The derived deformation functor DefX(A) = MapdAff(Spec A, X) for a connective E∞‑ring A is pro‑representable by the formal completion of the derived mapping stack, and its tangent complex at a point x is precisely LX ⊗L k(x). This perspective unifies the deformation theory of schemes, stacks, and even En‑algebras, and it is the starting point for the derived version of Artin’s representability theorem proved by Lurie and Toën–Vezzosi.

Applications appear throughout modern enumerative geometry. The virtual fundamental class of a proper derived moduli stack M with perfect obstruction theory E → LM is defined by intersecting the intrinsic normal cone with the zero section of the vector bundle stack h1/h0(E∨). When M = Mg,n(X,β) the moduli of stable maps, the obstruction theory comes from the relative cotangent complex of the universal curve, and the resulting invariants satisfy the expected gluing axioms. In derived symplectic geometry, the (−1)‑shifted symplectic structure on the derived critical locus of a function f: U → A1 is encoded by a non‑degenerate pairing on LCrit(f), leading to the AKSZ construction of topological quantum field theories. Examiners frequently test the distinction between the classical cotangent sheaf ΩX and the derived cotangent complex, the role of the transitivity triangle in base‑change problems, and the construction of virtual classes via perfect obstruction theories.

The Theory of Higher Chow Groups and Motivic Cohomology

Higher Chow groups CHp(X, q) were introduced by Bloch in 1986 as a geometric model for motivic cohomology. For a smooth quasi‑projective variety X over a field k, one considers the complex zp(X, •) of algebraic cycles of codimension p on X × Δ• meeting faces properly, where Δn = Spec k[t0,…,tn]/(∑ ti−1) is the algebraic n‑simplex. The homology of this complex in degree q defines CHp(X, q). When q = 0 one recovers the classical Chow group of codimension‑p cycles modulo rational equivalence. The groups are contravariant for flat pull‑backs and covariant for proper push‑forwards, and they carry a graded‑commutative product induced by the external product of cycles, making ⊕p,q CHp(X, q) a bigraded ring.

The Beilinson–Lichtenbaum conjecture, proved by Voevodsky (with contributions from Suslin, Friedlander, and others) in the early 2000s, identifies higher Chow groups with motivic cohomology: CHp(X, q) ≅ H2p−qM(X, ℤ(p)). Here ℤ(p) denotes the motivic complex, and the isomorphism is compatible with the cycle class map to étale cohomology after inverting the characteristic. This identification yields a Bloch–Kato type description of the Milnor K‑theory sheaf KMp as the Zariski sheaf associated to CHp(−, p). The norm‑residue isomorphism theorem (formerly the Bloch–Kato conjecture) follows as a corollary, linking Galois cohomology to Milnor K‑theory. In the ∞‑categorical language of motivic homotopy theory, the motivic sphere spectrum S represents the functor X ↦ ⊕p,q CHp(X, q) on the Morel–Voevodsky stable homotopy category SH(k).

Computations of higher Chow groups are notoriously difficult. For a smooth curve C over an algebraically closed field, CH1(C, 1) ≅ k× and CH2(C, 2) ≅ K2(k) by the work of Bloch and later Levine. For a surface S, the group CH2(S, 1) is related to the indecomposable part of K1 of the function field, and its torsion subgroup is controlled by the Brauer group of S. The moving lemma of Bloch–Levine ensures that the cycle complex computes the same groups after replacing Δ• by the cubical version, which is essential for the construction of the motivic spectral sequence converging to algebraic K‑theory. Examiners often ask for the definition of the cycle complex, the statement of the Beilinson–Lichtenbaum isomorphism, and the relationship between CHp(X, p) and Milnor K‑theory.

Computing a Higher Chow Group
Let X = Spec ℂ[t] be the affine line over ℂ. Compute CH1(X, 1) and explain why it vanishes.
The group CH1(X, 1) is the homology in degree 1 of the complex z1(X, •). A 1‑cycle on X × Δ1 of codimension 1 meeting faces properly is a finite sum of closed points on X × Δ1 not contained in the faces {t=0} or {t=1}. Since X is affine of dimension 1, any such cycle is a principal divisor of a rational function on X × Δ1 that is regular and invertible on the faces. By the homotopy invariance of higher Chow groups for smooth varieties (Bloch, 1986), the projection X × Δ1 → X induces an isomorphism CH1(X, 1) ≅ CH1(X, 0) = Pic(X) = 0 because the affine line has trivial Picard group. Hence CH1(X, 1) = 0.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a higher Chow group of an affine space, immediately invoke homotopy invariance: CHp(𝔸n, q) ≅ CHp(Spec k, q). The latter is known: it is Milnor K‑theory KMq(k) for p = q and zero otherwise. This reduces the computation to a standard algebraic K‑theory fact and avoids writing out the cycle complex.

The Theory of Factorization Homology and Extended Topological Field Theories

Factorization homology, developed by Lurie and independently by Ayala–Francis, provides a systematic way to integrate an En‑algebra over an n‑manifold. Given a framed n‑manifold M and an En‑algebra A in a symmetric monoidal ∞‑category C, the factorization homology ∫M A is the colimit of the factorization diagram that assigns to each disjoint union of disks embedded in M the tensor product of copies of A. When C = Chk (chain complexes over a field) and A is the En‑algebra of cochains on a based loop space, ∫M A computes the homology of the mapping space Map(M, X) for a simply connected space X. The construction satisfies excision: for a decomposition M = U ∪V W along a codimension‑0 submanifold V, there is a canonical equivalence ∫M A ≃ ∫U A ⊗∫V A ∫W A. This property makes factorization homology the natural target of the cobordism hypothesis.

The cobordism hypothesis of Baez–Dolan, proved by Lurie, states that the symmetric monoidal ∞‑category of fully extended n‑dimensional topological field theories with values in C is equivalent to the ∞‑groupoid of fully dualizable objects of C. An En‑algebra A that is fully dualizable determines a unique TFT ZA such that ZA(M) ≃ ∫M A for every closed n‑manifold M. In particular, the factorization homology of the n‑sphere Sn recovers the Hochschild homology of A as an En‑algebra, and the value on the n‑disk is A itself. For n = 2, an E2‑algebra is a braided monoidal category; factorization homology over a surface computes the Reshetikhin–Turaev invariants when A comes from a modular tensor category. The theory also extends to manifolds with boundary and corners, producing higher categories of boundary conditions and defects.

Recent work by Gwilliam–Scheimbauer and others has identified factorization homology with the observables of perturbative quantum field theories via the BV‑formalism. In this setting A is a factorization algebra of observables on ℝn, and ∫M A computes the space of global observables on M. The renormalization group flow corresponds to a deformation of the En‑structure, and the Costello–Gwilliam framework provides a rigorous construction of the effective BV‑action at each scale. Examiners test the definition of factorization homology as a colimit over the Ran space, the excision property, the statement of the cobordism hypothesis for fully dualizable En‑algebras, and the computation of ∫S1 A for an E1‑algebra (Hochschild homology).

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Analytic Geometry and Berkovich Spaces

Berkovich analytic spaces provide a topological framework for geometry over complete non‑archimedean fields such as ℚp or 𝔽q((t)). For a Banach algebra A over a non‑archimedean field k, the Berkovich spectrum M(A) is the set of multiplicative seminorms on A extending the absolute value on k, equipped with the weakest topology making the evaluation maps x ↦ |f(x)| continuous. Unlike Tate’s rigid analytic spaces, Berkovich spaces are locally compact, Hausdorff, and locally path‑connected; they contain the classical rigid points as a dense subset but also include “generic” points corresponding to Shilov boundaries of affinoid domains. The structure sheaf OX on a Berkovich space X is a sheaf of Banach algebras, and coherent sheaves behave analogously to the complex analytic case.

A fundamental result is the comparison theorem of Berkovich (1990) and later refined by Huber: the étale cohomology of a smooth rigid analytic variety coincides with the étale cohomology of its associated Berkovich space. This allows one to use the better topological properties of Berkovich spaces (e.g., existence of a strong deformation retraction onto a skeleton) to compute cohomology groups. The skeleton of a Berkovich curve is a finite graph whose vertices correspond to irreducible components of a semistable model; the retraction map is a homotopy equivalence. In higher dimensions, the theory of non‑archimedean pluripotential theory developed by Boucksom–Jonsson and others introduces Monge–Ampère measures on Berkovich spaces, enabling a variational approach to the Calabi–Yau problem and the construction of canonical metrics on line bundles.

Applications to p‑adic Hodge theory are profound. The period rings BdR, Bst, Bcris acquire natural structures as sheaves on the Berkovich analytic space associated to a p‑adic variety, and the p‑adic comparison isomorphisms (Faltings, Tsuji, Scholze) can be formulated as isomorphisms of sheaves on the pro‑étale site of the Berkovich space. Scholze’s perfectoid spaces are a special class of adic spaces that are locally isomorphic to Spa(A, A+) with A perfectoid; they embed into the category of Berkovich spaces via the functor sending a perfectoid algebra to its Berkovich spectrum. Examiners often ask for the definition of the Berkovich spectrum, the distinction between type‑1 (classical) and type‑2,3,4 points, the existence of skeleta for curves, and the role of the Shilov boundary in the maximum modulus principle.

The Theory of Arithmetic Dynamics and Canonical Heights

Arithmetic dynamics studies the iteration of rational maps φ: ℙN → ℙN defined over a number field K. The canonical height ĥφ(P) introduced by Call and Silverman (1993) is the limit ĥφ(P) = limn→∞ h(φn(P))/dn, where h is a Weil height and d = deg φ. This height satisfies ĥφ(φ(P)) = d·ĥφ(P) and differs from any Weil height by a bounded function. The Northcott property holds: for any bound B, the set {P ∈ ℙN(K) : ĥφ(P) ≤ B} is finite. Consequently, preperiodic points (those with finite forward orbit) are exactly the points of canonical height zero.

Equidistribution theorems of Yuan, Baker–Rumely, and Favre–Rivera‑Letelier describe the asymptotic distribution of small points. For a sequence of distinct points Pn with ĥφ(Pn) → 0, the Galois orbits equidistribute towards the equilibrium measure μφ on the Berkovich projective line at each place. Over ℂ, μφ is the unique measure of maximal entropy log d; over a non‑archimedean field it is supported on the Julia set in the Berkovich space. This equidistribution underpins the proof of the dynamical Manin–Mumford conjecture (Ghioca–Tucker–Zieve) and the dynamical Bogomolov conjecture (Favre–Gauthier). The latter asserts that a subvariety V ⊂ ℙN contains a Zariski‑dense set of preperiodic points only if V is preperiodic under φ.

Canonical heights also control the arithmetic of dynatomic polynomials. For a rational map φ of degree d, the n‑th dynatomic polynomial Φn,φ(x) parametrizes points of exact period n. The height of its roots is related to the canonical height of the corresponding periodic points, and the Mahler measure of Φn,φ grows like dn. In the case of polynomial maps f(z) = zd + c, the bifurcation locus in the parameter space (the Mandelbrot set for d = 2) can be characterized as the support of the bifurcation current Tbif = ddc ĥf(c), where ĥf(c) is the canonical height of the critical point. Examiners test the definition and basic properties of the canonical height, the Northcott finiteness, the equidistribution statement at archimedean and non‑archimedean places, and the characterization of preperiodic subvarieties via the dynamical Bogomolov conjecture.

  • Confusing the cotangent complex with the classical Kähler differentials; the former lives in the derived category and captures higher obstruction information.
  • Assuming higher Chow groups agree with ordinary Chow groups for all q; they vanish for q > 0 on affine space but can be non‑zero on general varieties.
  • Treating factorization homology as ordinary homology of a manifold; it depends on the En‑algebra input and satisfies excision, not just homotopy invariance.
  • Identifying Berkovich type‑1 points with all points of the space; type‑2,3,4 points are essential for the topology and for the maximum modulus principle.
  • Believing canonical height zero implies a point is periodic; it only implies preperiodicity (finite forward orbit).
  • Neglecting the role of the equilibrium measure in equidistribution; the measure is the unique measure of maximal entropy and its support is the Julia set.
  • Overlooking the distinction between the dynamical Manin–Mumford and Bogomolov conjectures; the former concerns torsion points on semi‑abelian varieties, the latter concerns preperiodic points for polarizable maps.

The advanced sections above integrate derived, motivic, topological, non‑archimedean, and dynamical methods into a coherent toolkit for modern research problems.

The Theory of Arithmetic Dynamics and Canonical Heights

Arithmetic dynamics studies the iteration of rational maps φ : ℙⁿ → ℙⁿ defined over a number field K. The central invariant is the canonical height ĥ_φ(P) introduced by Call and Silverman (1993). For a point P ∈ ℙⁿ(K) and a Weil height h associated to a divisor of degree one, the canonical height is defined as the limit ĥ_φ(P) = limm→∞ h(φ^m(P)) / d^m, where d = deg φ. This limit exists and satisfies the functional equation ĥ_φ(φ(P)) = d·ĥ_φ(P). Moreover, ĥ_φ differs from any Weil height by a bounded function on ℙⁿ(K).

The Northcott property holds: for any bound B, the set { P ∈ ℙⁿ(K) : ĥ_φ(P) ≤ B } is finite. Consequently, a point is preperiodic (its forward orbit is finite) if and only if its canonical height is zero. This characterisation is the dynamical analogue of the classical theorem of Néron–Tate for abelian varieties.

Equidistribution theorems describe the asymptotic distribution of points of small canonical height. Over an archimedean place, Yuan (2008) proved that for a sequence of distinct points P_m with ĥ_φ(P_m) → 0, the Galois orbits equidistribute towards the unique measure of maximal entropy μ_φ on the complex projective space, which is the equilibrium measure of φ. Over a non‑archimedean place, Baker–Rumely (2006) and Favre–Rivera‑Letelier (2006) established equidistribution on the Berkovich projective line; the limiting measure is supported on the Julia set in the Berkovich space and coincides with the measure of maximal entropy log d.

These results underpin major conjectures. The dynamical Manin–Mumford conjecture (proved by Ghioca–Tucker–Zieve) asserts that a subvariety containing a Zariski‑dense set of preperiodic points must be preperiodic under φ. The dynamical Bogomolov conjecture (Favre–Gauthier) predicts the same conclusion for polarizable maps. Canonical heights also control the arithmetic of dynatomic polynomials Φn,φ(x) whose roots are points of exact period n. The Mahler measure of Φn,φ grows like d^n, and for unicritical polynomials f_c(z)=z^d+c the bifurcation current Tbif=dd^c ĥf_c(c) has support equal to the bifurcation locus (the Mandelbrot set when d=2).

The Theory of Non‑Archimedean Geometry and Berkovich Spaces

Berkovich analytic spaces provide a locally compact, path‑connected framework for geometry over a complete non‑archimedean field K. For a K-affinoid algebra A, the Berkovich spectrum M(A) is the set of multiplicative seminorms |·|_x on A extending the absolute value on K, equipped with the weakest topology making the evaluation maps x ↦ |f|_x continuous for all f ∈ A. Points of M(A) are classified into four types: type‑1 points correspond to classical rigid‑analytic points (maximal ideals); type‑2 points are seminorms with value group equal to |K^×| and residue field a finite extension of the residue field of K; type‑3 points have value group strictly larger than |K^×| but residue field equal to the residue field of K; type‑4 points have both larger value group and larger residue field. Types 2–4 have no classical counterpart and are essential for the topology and for the maximum modulus principle, which states that a bounded analytic function on a connected affinoid domain attains its maximum on the Shilov boundary, a canonical finite subset of type‑2 points.

For a smooth projective curve X over K, the Berkovich space Xan admits a skeleton — a finite graph obtained by retracting onto the union of type‑2 points corresponding to semistable models. This skeleton carries a canonical metric and encodes the reduction graph of a semistable model. The theory extends to higher dimensions via adic spaces (Huber) and perfectoid spaces (Scholze). Perfectoid algebras are complete Tate algebras over a perfectoid field whose Frobenius is surjective on the tilt; their Berkovich spectra embed into the category of adic spaces. The pro‑étale site of a perfectoid space carries the period sheaves BdR, Bst, Bcris, and the p‑adic comparison isomorphisms (Faltings, Tsuji, Scholze) become isomorphisms of sheaves on this site.

Examiners frequently test the definition of the Berkovich spectrum, the distinction among the four point types, the existence and properties of skeleta for curves, and the role of the Shilov boundary in the maximum modulus principle. A typical question asks to prove that a bounded analytic function on a connected affinoid domain attains its supremum on the Shilov boundary, or to describe the retraction map onto the skeleton of a Mumford curve.

Worked Example: Canonical Height for a Unicritical Polynomial
Let f_c(z)=z2+c with c ∈ ℚ. Compute the canonical height ĥf_c(0) of the critical point 0 and explain its relation to the bifurcation current.
The canonical height of the critical point is ĥf_c(0) = limn→∞ h(f_c^n(0))/2^n, where h is the standard logarithmic Weil height on ℚ. For each n, f_c^n(0) is a polynomial in c with integer coefficients; its height grows like 2^n ĥf_c(0). The bifurcation current is Tbif=dd^c ĥf_c(c) (here c is the parameter). The support of Tbif is exactly the bifurcation locus in the parameter space, which for d=2 is the Mandelbrot set. Thus ĥf_c(0) is a potential function for the bifurcation current, and its Laplacian measures the distribution of parameters where the dynamics of the critical point is unstable.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a property of Berkovich points, first recall the four‑type classification and the definition of the Shilov boundary. For canonical heights, write down the limit definition and the functional equation ĥ_φ(φ(P))=d·ĥ_φ(P); then invoke Northcott finiteness to deduce preperiodicity from height zero. In equidistribution problems, distinguish archimedean (Yuan) from non‑archimedean (Baker–Rumely, Favre–Rivera‑Letelier) statements and cite the relevant measure (maximal entropy vs. equilibrium measure on the Berkovich line). Keep a one‑page cheat sheet with these three pillars: definition, functional equation, Northcott; point types, skeleton, Shilov boundary; equidistribution theorems and their measures.

The Theory of Derived Deformation Theory and the Cotangent Complex

Derived deformation theory replaces classical functors of Artin rings by functors on the ∞‑category of derived Artinian algebras. The central object is the cotangent complex LB/A of a morphism of commutative rings A → B, constructed by Illusie (1971) as a derived functor of Kähler differentials. Unlike the module of Kähler differentials ΩB/A, which only captures first‑order information, LB/A lives in the derived category D(B) and encodes higher obstruction classes. For a square‑zero extension B' → B with kernel I, the obstruction to lifting a map A → B lies in Ext2_B(LB/A, I); the space of lifts, when non‑empty, is a torsor under Ext1_B(LB/A, I).

Lurie's reformulation (Higher Algebra, 2017) expresses the cotangent complex as the left derived functor of the abelianization functor from the ∞‑category of A-algebras to A-modules. This perspective yields a natural Postnikov tower for LB/A whose truncations recover the André–Quillen homology groups D^q(B/A, M). The cotangent complex satisfies fundamental exact triangles: for composable maps A → B → C there is a distinguished triangle LB/A ⊗_B C → LC/A → LC/B →. When B is a complete intersection over A, LB/A is perfect of Tor‑amplitude in [−1,0]; this characterisation underpins the derived version of the local complete intersection property.

Applications include the derived construction of the moduli stack of perfect complexes on a scheme, where the tangent complex at a point E is RHom(E,E)[1] and the obstruction theory is governed by RHom(E,E)[2]. In derived algebraic geometry, the cotangent complex of a derived scheme X provides a perfect obstruction theory for the truncation t0 X, enabling virtual fundamental classes in enumerative geometry (Behrend–Fantechi). Examiners often ask for the definition of LB/A via simplicial resolutions, the exact triangle for composable maps, and the interpretation of Ext^i groups as obstruction and deformation spaces.

The Theory of Higher Stacks and Artin's Representability

Higher stacks generalize algebraic stacks by allowing values in ∞‑groupoids rather than ordinary groupoids. An n‑stack on a site C is a presheaf of (∞,1)‑categories satisfying descent for hypercovers. Artin's representability theorem (1974) gives criteria for a functor F : (Aff/S)op → Groupoids to be represented by an algebraic stack: F must be a sheaf for the étale topology, have representable diagonal, satisfy Schlessinger's conditions (H1)–(H4) on deformation functors, and admit a formally smooth cover by a scheme. In the derived setting, Lurie (Derived Algebraic Geometry V) extends these criteria to functors valued in spaces (∞‑groupoids). The key input is a cotangent complex for the functor, which controls the obstruction theory via the same Ext groups as in classical deformation theory.

A derived stack X is geometric if it admits a representable, locally of finite presentation, and relatively perfect morphism from a disjoint union of derived affine schemes (an atlas). The truncation t0 X is a classical algebraic stack, and the higher homotopy groups of the mapping spaces encode derived structure. For example, the derived moduli stack of perfect complexes on a smooth projective variety is geometric; its truncation is the classical moduli stack of perfect complexes, while the derived enhancement remembers the full Ext groups. Artin's criteria in the derived context require the functor to be nilcomplete, infinitesimally cohesive, and to have a cotangent complex that is perfect and connective.

Examiners test the distinction between classical and derived stacks, the role of the cotangent complex in the derived Artin representability theorem, and the construction of the derived moduli of perfect complexes. A typical question asks to verify Schlessinger's condition (H2) for the deformation functor of a coherent sheaf, or to explain why the derived stack of perfect complexes admits a perfect obstruction theory given by the cotangent complex.

The Theory of Motivic Integration and the Denef–Loeser Formula

Motivic integration, introduced by Kontsevich (1995) and developed by Denef–Loeser (1999), assigns a measure with values in the Grothendieck ring of varieties K0(Var_K) to definable subsets of the arc space X_∞ of a smooth variety X over a field K of characteristic zero. The motivic measure μ is defined on cylinders π_n-1(C) (where π_n : X_∞ → X_n is the truncation to jets of order n) by μ(π_n-1(C)) = [C]·𝕃-n·dim X, with 𝕃 = [𝔸1]. This measure extends uniquely to a σ‑algebra of stable subsets.

The change‑of‑variables formula of Denef–Loeser states that for a proper birational morphism f : Y → X with Y smooth, and a measurable subset A ⊂ X_∞, one has ∫_A 𝕃-ord_Jac(f) dμ_X = ∫f_∞-1(A) dμ_Y, where ord_Jac(f) is the order of vanishing of the Jacobian determinant along arcs. This formula yields the motivic zeta function Zmot(T) = ∫X_∞ 𝕃-ord(f) Tord(f) dμ for a regular function f, which specializes to the topological, Hodge, and Igusa p‑adic zeta functions via suitable ring homomorphisms from K0(Var_K).

Applications include the proof of the McKay correspondence for finite subgroups of SL_n(ℂ) (Batyrev, Denef–Loeser), the computation of stringy Hodge numbers of log terminal pairs, and the invariance of the motivic volume under birational transformations of Calabi–Yau varieties. Examiners often ask for the definition of the motivic measure on cylinders, the statement of the change‑of‑variables formula, and the specialization to the Hodge–Deligne polynomial. A typical problem: given a hypersurface singularity f = x2 + y3, compute its motivic zeta function in K0(Var_ℂ)[[T]] and deduce the Hodge spectrum.

  • Confusing the canonical height with a Weil height; the canonical height is the limit of normalized Weil heights and satisfies the exact functional equation.
  • Assuming all points of canonical height zero are periodic; they are only preperiodic (finite forward orbit).
  • Identifying Berkovich type‑1 points with the whole space; types 2–4 are essential for compactness, skeleta, and the maximum modulus principle.
  • Neglecting the Shilov boundary when applying the maximum modulus principle on affinoid domains.
  • Treating the cotangent complex as the module of Kähler differentials; the former lives in the derived category and captures higher obstructions.
