hand/graph-theory.html:
Graph Minors and the Robertson–Seymour Theorem

The theory of graph minors, developed by Neil Robertson and Paul Seymour over a series of twenty‑three papers published between 1983 and 2004, provides a structural decomposition for any graph that excludes a fixed minor. A graph H is a minor of G if H can be obtained from G by deleting vertices, deleting edges, and contracting edges. The Robertson–Seymour theorem states that for every finite set of graphs there are only finitely many minimal excluded minors; equivalently, the class of graphs that do not contain any graph from a fixed finite set as a minor is well‑quasi‑ordered under the minor relation. This deep result implies that any property of graphs that is closed under taking minors can be characterized by a finite list of forbidden minors. For example, planar graphs are exactly those that exclude K₅ and K₃,₃ as minors (Wagner’s theorem, 1937), and graphs of treewidth at most k are precisely those that exclude the (k+2)‑clique as a minor. The proof uses a sophisticated “structure theorem” showing that any H‑minor‑free graph can be built by clique‑sums of pieces that are “almost embeddable” on a surface of bounded genus. Algorithmic consequences are profound: for every fixed H, testing whether a given graph contains H as a minor can be done in cubic time (O(n³)), and many NP‑hard problems become polynomial on H‑minor‑free classes via dynamic programming on the decomposition. The theorem also underpins the graph minor algorithm used in the proof of the four‑color theorem’s computer‑assisted verification.

Spectral Graph Theory — Eigenvalues, Expanders, and Mixing

Spectral graph theory studies the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices associated with a graph, most commonly the adjacency matrix A and the Laplacian matrix L = D − A where D is the diagonal degree matrix. For a d‑regular graph, the largest eigenvalue of A is d, and the second‑largest eigenvalue λ₂ controls expansion: the edge‑expansion h(G) satisfies (d − λ₂)/2 ≤ h(G) ≤ √(2d(d − λ₂)) (Cheeger inequality, 1970). Graphs with a large spectral gap d − λ₂ are called expanders; they have the property that every small vertex set has many edges leaving it. Explicit constructions of constant‑degree expanders were given by Margulis (1973) and later by Lubotzky‑Phillips‑Sarnak (1988) using Ramanujan graphs, which achieve the optimal bound λ₂ ≤ 2√(d−1). Expanders are central to derandomization, error‑correcting codes (e.g., LDPC codes), and the construction of pseudorandom generators. The mixing time of a random walk on a graph is also governed by the spectral gap: the total variation distance to the stationary distribution after t steps decays as O((λ₂/d)ᵗ). For non‑regular graphs the normalized Laplacian ℒ = D⁻¹ᐟ² L D⁻¹ᐟ² has eigenvalues 0 = μ₁ ≤ μ₂ ≤ … ≤ μₙ ≤ 2, and the same Cheeger‑type bounds hold with μ₂ playing the role of the spectral gap. Applications range from clustering (spectral partitioning using the Fiedler vector) to the analysis of social networks and the design of fast solvers for linear systems (Laplacian solvers).

Worked Example — Spectral Gap of a Cycle
Compute the second‑largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix of the cycle Cₙ and deduce its edge‑expansion up to constant factors.
The adjacency matrix of Cₙ has eigenvalues 2 cos(2πk/n) for k = 0,…,n−1. The largest is 2 (k=0). The second‑largest is 2 cos(2π/n) = 2 − (2π²/n²) + O(1/n⁴). Hence the spectral gap d − λ₂ = 2 − 2 cos(2π/n) ≈ 4π²/n². By Cheeger’s inequality, the edge‑expansion h(Cₙ) satisfies (d − λ₂)/2 ≤ h ≤ √(2d(d − λ₂)). Substituting gives Θ(1/n²) ≤ h ≤ Θ(1/n). The exact expansion of a cycle is 2/n, confirming the lower bound is tight up to a factor of n. This illustrates that cycles are poor expanders: their spectral gap shrinks quadratically with n.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for expansion or mixing time, first identify whether the graph is regular. If it is, write down the Cheeger inequality and the relation between λ₂ and the spectral gap. For non‑regular graphs, switch to the normalized Laplacian and use μ₂. Remember that explicit eigenvalues are known for paths, cycles, complete graphs, and hypercubes; memorize these four spectra to avoid recomputation under time pressure.

Graph Homomorphisms and the Chromatic Polynomial

A homomorphism from a graph G to a graph H is a vertex mapping f: V(G) → V(H) such that every edge uv ∈ E(G) maps to an edge f(u)f(v) ∈ E(H). The existence of a homomorphism G → Kₖ is equivalent to a proper k‑coloring of G, so the chromatic number χ(G) is the smallest k with a homomorphism to Kₖ. The chromatic polynomial P_G(k) counts the number of proper k‑colorings for integer k ≥ 0; it is a polynomial in k of degree |V(G)| with integer coefficients alternating in sign. Deletion‑contraction gives the recurrence P_G(k) = PG−e(k) − PG/e(k) for any edge e, which yields an algorithm exponential in the number of edges but polynomial for graphs of bounded treewidth. The zeros of P_G(k) in the complex plane (chromatic roots) have been studied extensively; Birkhoff and Lewis (1946) conjectured that no chromatic root lies in the interval (0, 4) for planar graphs, a statement equivalent to the four‑color theorem. Tutte (1970) introduced the bivariate Tutte polynomial T_G(x, y), which specializes to the chromatic polynomial via P_G(k) = (−1)|V|−c(G) kc(G) T_G(1−k, 0) where c(G) is the number of components. The Tutte polynomial also evaluates to the number of spanning trees (T_G(1,1)), the reliability polynomial (T_G(1, p/(1−p))), and the partition function of the q‑state Potts model. Computing T_G is #P‑hard in general, but fixed‑parameter tractable with respect to treewidth.

Treewidth, Parameterized Algorithms, and Courcelle’s Theorem

Treewidth measures how close a graph is to a tree. A tree decomposition of G is a pair (T, {X_t}t∈V(T)) where T is a tree and each bag X_t ⊆ V(G) satisfies: (1) every vertex appears in some bag, (2) for every edge uv there is a bag containing both u and v, (3) for each vertex v the bags containing v form a connected subtree of T. The width is max_t |X_t| − 1; the treewidth tw(G) is the minimum width over all decompositions. Trees have treewidth 1, cycles have treewidth 2, and the k×k grid has treewidth k. Many NP‑hard problems become linear‑time solvable on graphs of bounded treewidth via dynamic programming on a nice tree decomposition (e.g., Hamiltonian cycle, 3‑coloring, independent set). Courcelle’s theorem (1990) gives a meta‑result: any graph property expressible in monadic second‑order logic (MSO₂) can be decided in time f(φ, tw)·n for a fixed formula φ, where f is a computable function depending only on φ and the treewidth. This includes properties like “G has a Hamiltonian cycle” (expressible in MSO₂) and “G is 3‑colorable”. The theorem is non‑constructive because the constant f grows as a tower of exponentials in the quantifier depth of φ, but it establishes fixed‑parameter tractability for a vast class of problems. Recent work on rank‑width and clique‑width extends similar algorithmic meta‑theorems to dense graphs.

The Tutte Polynomial — Universality and Network Reliability

The Tutte polynomial T_G(x, y) = ΣA⊆E (x−1)c(A)−c(E) (y−1)c(A)+|A|−|V| where c(A) is the number of connected components of the subgraph (V, A), is the most general graph invariant satisfying a deletion‑contraction recurrence. It specializes to numerous combinatorial quantities: the chromatic polynomial P_G(k) = (−1)|V|−c(G) kc(G) T_G(1−k, 0); the flow polynomial F_G(k) = (−1)|E|−|V|+c(G) T_G(0, 1−k); the number of spanning trees τ(G) = T_G(1, 1); the reliability polynomial R_G(p) = (1−p)|E|−|V|+c(G) p|V|−c(G) T_G(1, 1/p). Evaluating T_G at (2, 1) gives the number of spanning forests, at (1, 2) the number of connected spanning subgraphs, and at (2, 0) the number of acyclic orientations. The computational complexity of exact evaluation is #P‑hard for almost all points (x, y) except a few tractable lines (e.g., (1,1), (2,1), (1,2), (0,−1)). Approximation via Markov chain Monte Carlo (the Jerrum‑Sinclair algorithm) yields a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS) for the ferromagnetic Potts model region (x>1, y>1). In network reliability, edges fail independently with probability 1−p; the probability that the surviving graph remains connected is exactly R_G(p). The Tutte polynomial thus unifies coloring, flows, reliability, and statistical physics, making it a central object in algebraic graph theory.

  • Confusing minor‑closed with subgraph‑closed properties — minors allow edge contractions, subgraphs do not.
  • Assuming every expander is Ramanujan — Ramanujan graphs achieve the optimal spectral bound, but many expanders have larger λ₂.
  • Treating the chromatic polynomial as a proper coloring count for non‑integer arguments — P_G(k) only counts colorings when k is a non‑negative integer.
  • Believing Courcelle’s theorem gives practical algorithms — the hidden constant is nonelementary, so it is a classification tool, not an implementation guide.
  • Evaluating the Tutte polynomial at arbitrary points without checking the known tractable loci — most evaluations are #P‑hard.
  • Overlooking that treewidth of a grid grows with its side length, so planar graphs can have arbitrarily large treewidth.
The advanced topics above complete the core theoretical toolkit needed for research‑level graph theory examinations.

Edge Connectivity, Menger’s Theorem and Network Reliability

While the Max‑Flow Min‑Cut theorem relates a single source–sink pair to the capacity of a cut, edge‑connectivity generalises the idea to arbitrary vertex pairs. The edge‑connectivity κ′(G) of a graph G is the minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects G. Equivalently, κ′(G) is the size of a smallest edge‑cut. Menger’s theorem (1927) provides a precise combinatorial characterisation: for any two distinct vertices u and v, the maximum number of pairwise edge‑disjoint u‑v paths equals the minimum size of an edge‑cut separating u from v. When this holds for every pair, the common value is κ′(G).

Computationally, κ′(G) can be obtained by running a max‑flow algorithm on the graph with unit capacities, once for each vertex pair, and taking the minimum flow value. More efficiently, the Nagamochi‑Ibaraki algorithm computes κ′(G) in O(m + n) time by repeatedly contracting edges while preserving the minimum cut size.

Edge‑connectivity has direct implications for network reliability. In the classical reliability model, each edge fails independently with probability q. The probability that the network stays connected is the all‑terminal reliability R(G,q). For small κ′(G), the dominant failure events are the removal of a minimum cut. An approximation R(G,q) ≈ 1 − C·qκ′(G) (where C is the number of distinct minimum cuts) is often sufficient for exam‑level estimation. The number of minimum cuts in a simple graph is bounded by O(n2κ′−2) (Cunningham, 1985), a fact that can be invoked to argue about the order of magnitude of reliability for highly connected networks.

Exam‑writers frequently test the ability to move between the three equivalent statements of Menger’s theorem: (i) edge‑disjoint paths, (ii) size of a minimum edge‑cut, and (iii) the value of a max‑flow with unit capacities. A typical twist is to give a graph with a specified κ′(G) and ask for the maximum number of edge‑disjoint spanning trees, which by Nash‑Williams/Tutte theorem equals ⌊κ′(G)/2⌋. Recognising that a 4‑edge‑connected planar graph admits two edge‑disjoint spanning trees can earn full credit.

Graph Minors Beyond Robertson–Seymour – Well‑Quasi‑Ordering and Algorithmic Consequences

The Robertson–Seymour theorem (2004) famously states that the set of finite undirected graphs is well‑quasi‑ordered (WQO) under the minor relation: any infinite sequence of graphs contains a pair where the earlier is a minor of the later. This deep structural result yields two practical corollaries for competitive examinations.

First, any minor‑closed property 𝒫 (e.g., “planarity”, “treewidth ≤ k”, “no K₅ minor”) can be characterised by a finite obstruction set ℱ𝒫: a graph belongs to 𝒫 iff it contains none of the graphs in ℱ𝒫 as a minor. For planarity, ℱ𝒫 = {K₅, K₃,₃}. For graphs of treewidth at most 2, ℱ𝒫 consists of the 3‑cycle with a chord and the complete graph K₄. Knowing these obstruction sets allows a quick “yes/no” decision by checking for the presence of a small forbidden minor, a technique often hidden in exam questions that present a seemingly large graph and ask whether it satisfies a minor‑closed property.

Second, the theorem implies the existence of an algorithmic meta‑theorem: any property definable in monadic second‑order logic (MSO₁) can be decided in cubic time on graphs of bounded treewidth. While Courcelle’s theorem (covered earlier) handles MSO₂, the minor‑closed perspective gives a complementary route. For instance, the property “graph is series‑parallel” is MSO₁‑definable and, because series‑parallel graphs exclude K₄ as a minor, they have treewidth ≤ 2. Consequently, a linear‑time algorithm exists to test series‑parallelness by first verifying the absence of a K₄ minor (using a depth‑first search based minor‑testing routine) and then applying a simple series‑parallel reduction.

Exam‑level questions may combine these ideas: present a graph and ask whether it can be reduced to a tree by a sequence of edge deletions and contractions that never creates a K₃,₃ minor. The correct approach is to argue that the graph must be planar and have treewidth ≤ 2, then invoke the finite obstruction set for treewidth‑2 graphs. A common twist is to give a graph that is planar but contains a K₄ minor; students who stop at planarity will lose marks, whereas recognising the need to check the K₄ obstruction yields the right answer.

Technique: Minor‑Closed Obstruction Checking
Given a simple graph G with 12 vertices and 18 edges, determine whether G can be embedded on a torus without edge crossings. Justify your answer using minor theory.

The torus admits all planar graphs plus those that contain a K₅ or K₃,₃ minor but no higher‑genus obstruction. The minimal forbidden minors for genus‑1 (the torus) are known: they are the 7 graphs listed by Archdeacon (1981), the smallest of which is K₇. Since G has only 12 vertices and 18 edges, its average degree is 3, far below the minimum degree 6 required for K₇. Moreover, a quick search for K₅ or K₃,₃ minors fails because any 5‑vertex subgraph has at most 9 edges, insufficient for K₅, and any bipartite 3‑3 subgraph would need 9 edges, which does not appear. Hence G contains none of the torus‑forbidden minors and therefore can be embedded on a torus.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about embeddability or a minor‑closed property, first list the known obstruction set for the relevant surface or width bound. Then scan the given graph for those small patterns; a quick degree count often eliminates larger obstructions. If time permits, perform a contraction‑deletion test on the suspected subgraph to confirm the presence or absence of the minor.

Algebraic Connectivity, Spectral Gaps and the Cheeger Inequality

The Laplacian matrix L = D − A (where D is the degree diagonal matrix and A the adjacency matrix) encodes many global properties of a graph. Its eigenvalues satisfy 0 = λ₁ ≤ λ₂ ≤ … ≤ λ_n. The second smallest eigenvalue λ₂, called the algebraic connectivity, measures how well‑connected the graph is. A classic result by Fiedler (1973) shows that λ₂ > 0 iff the graph is connected, and larger λ₂ indicates stronger connectivity.

The Cheeger inequality links λ₂ to the isoperimetric constant h(G), defined as

h(G) = minS⊂V, 0<|S|≤|V|/2 (|∂S| / |S|),

where ∂S is the set of edges leaving S. The inequality states

2 h(G) ≥ λ₂ ≥ h(G)² / (2 Δ),

with Δ the maximum degree. This provides a two‑sided bound: a small λ₂ guarantees the existence of a sparse cut, while a large λ₂ forces every cut to be relatively dense. In exam settings, students are often asked to estimate h(G) for a regular graph given λ₂, or conversely to bound λ₂ from a known expansion property.

Applications include network design: to guarantee resilience against edge failures, one may aim for λ₂ ≥ c·log n, which for d‑regular graphs implies an edge‑expansion of Θ(d). Conversely, in clustering problems, the Fiedler vector (the eigenvector corresponding to λ₂) is used to partition the vertex set by sign, yielding a cut whose size is within a factor of 2 of the optimum Cheeger cut (spectral partitioning algorithm).

Exam writers sometimes disguise the inequality: they may give the Laplacian eigenvalues of a 5‑vertex graph and ask for the minimum number of edges that must be removed to disconnect it. The correct method is to note that λ₂ > 0, compute h(G) ≤ √(2 Δ λ₂), and then infer that any cut must delete at least h(G)·⌊n/2⌋ edges. A common trap is to confuse λ₂ with the spectral radius (largest eigenvalue of A); the former governs connectivity, the latter governs degree‑related properties.

Parameterized Complexity of Subgraph Isomorphism and the Color‑Coding Technique

Finding a fixed pattern H as a subgraph of a larger host graph G is NP‑complete in general (the Subgraph Isomorphism problem). Parameterised complexity studies the problem with respect to a natural parameter k = |V(H)|. The classic result by Alon, Yuster and Zwick (1995) introduced the color‑coding method, showing that for any fixed k, one can detect a k‑vertex subgraph isomorphic to H in time O(ek·nO(1)), i.e., fixed‑parameter tractable (FPT).

The technique works by randomly assigning each vertex of G a colour from {1,…,k}. With probability k! / kk ≥ e−k, a particular copy of H receives a proper colouring (each vertex of H gets a distinct colour). By repeating the random colouring O(ek) times, the probability of missing the desired copy becomes negligible. For each colouring, dynamic programming over a tree‑decomposition of H (or a simple DP for paths and cycles) checks whether a colour‑preserving embedding exists.

Deterministic colour‑coding uses families of k‑perfect hash functions (k‑wise independent families) of size O(ek·log n), guaranteeing that at least one colouring is perfect for every possible embedding. This derandomisation is essential for exam questions that explicitly ask for a deterministic algorithm.

Important extensions include the use of colour‑coding for finding simple paths of length k (the k‑Path problem) and for detecting bounded‑treewidth patterns. The running time improves to O(2O(k)·n) for paths, and to O( f(k)·n ) for any pattern of treewidth t, where f depends only on k and t. Recognising when a pattern has bounded treewidth allows the examinee to replace the generic O(ek) bound with a sharper O(2k) bound.

Typical exam twists: a question may present a host graph with maximum degree Δ and ask for the complexity of detecting a k‑vertex star K1,k. Since a star has treewidth 1, the problem is solvable in O(Δ·n) time, independent of k, by simply scanning neighbourhoods. Another variant asks to prove that detecting a k‑clique cannot be solved in time f(k)·no(k) unless the Exponential Time Hypothesis fails; the answer hinges on the known lower bound for k‑Clique and the fact that colour‑coding does not improve beyond O(nk) for dense patterns.

  • Confusing edge‑connectivity κ′(G) with vertex‑connectivity κ(G); the two coincide only for regular graphs.
  • Applying Menger’s theorem to directed graphs without checking the appropriate version (edge‑disjoint vs. internally vertex‑disjoint paths).
  • Assuming that any minor‑closed property has a single forbidden minor; most have a finite but larger obstruction set.
  • Using the Cheeger inequality with λ₁ instead of λ₂, which leads to a trivial bound.
  • Treating the spectral radius of the adjacency matrix as a measure of connectivity, ignoring the role of the Laplacian eigenvalues.
  • Neglecting the derandomisation step in colour‑coding and claiming the random algorithm is always acceptable for exact answers.
  • Believing that a bounded‑degree host graph automatically yields a polynomial‑time subgraph isomorphism algorithm for any fixed pattern, overlooking the pattern’s treewidth.

hand/set-theory.html:
Forcing and the Independence of the Continuum Hypothesis

Paul Cohen introduced forcing in 1963 to prove that the Continuum Hypothesis (CH) is independent of ZFC. The method builds a generic extension V[G] of a ground model V by adjoining a generic filter G for a partially ordered set (poset) ℙ. The elements of ℙ are called conditions; a filter G ⊆ ℙ is generic over V if it meets every dense subset of ℙ that belongs to V. The forcing relation ⊩ defines when a condition forces a statement to hold in the extension. Cohen’s original poset for adding a new subset of ω consists of finite partial functions from ω to 2 ordered by reverse inclusion. The generic filter yields a Cohen real, a new subset of ω not in V, and the extension satisfies ¬CH while preserving all cardinals and cofinalities. The Boolean-valued model approach, developed by Scott, Solovay, and Vopěnka, replaces the poset by a complete Boolean algebra ℬ and interprets formulas as Boolean truth values; generic ultrafilters on ℬ then produce the same extensions. Easton’s theorem (1970) shows that the continuum function κ ↦ 2^κ on regular cardinals can be prescribed arbitrarily subject to monotonicity and König’s lemma, demonstrating the vast flexibility of forcing. Iterated forcing with countable support preserves ω₁ and allows the construction of models where the continuum is ℵ₂, ℵ_ω₁, or any regular cardinal above ℵ₁. Proper forcing, introduced by Shelah, preserves stationary subsets of ω₁ and is essential for preserving combinatorial principles such as ◊ and □. The technique also proves the independence of the Axiom of Choice from ZF by adding a generic set of atoms (Fraenkel–Mostowski models) or by symmetric submodels of forcing extensions. Forcing has become the central tool for exploring the landscape of set‑theoretic universes and for calibrating the consistency strength of mathematical statements.

The Constructible Universe L and Inner Model Theory

Gödel’s constructible universe L, defined in 1938, is the smallest transitive class containing all ordinals and closed under definable power set operations. Formally, L₀ = ∅, Lα+1 = Def(L_α) (the set of subsets of L_α definable over ⟨L_α,∈⟩ with parameters), and L_λ = ⋃α<λ L_α for limit λ; L = ⋃α∈Ord L_α. Gödel proved that L satisfies ZFC and the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis (GCH). The Condensation Lemma states that any elementary substructure of some L_α is isomorphic to some L_β, which yields fine structural control over L. Jensen’s fine structure theory (1972) introduced the Σ_n hierarchy over L, the projectum, and the master code, enabling the analysis of large cardinal properties inside L. The Covering Lemma for L asserts that every uncountable set of ordinals is covered by a constructible set of the same cardinality, provided 0^♯ does not exist. If 0^♯ exists, L is “thin” and there are many indiscernibles, leading to a rich hierarchy of inner models for measurable cardinals (the Dodd–Jensen core model K). Inner model theory builds canonical models L[U] for a measurable cardinal, L[μ] for a strong cardinal, and ultimately the core model K below a Woodin cardinal. These models satisfy ZFC and capture the large cardinal structure up to their level. The existence of 0^♯ is equivalent to the existence of a non‑trivial elementary embedding j: L → L, and its consistency strength is strictly below a measurable cardinal. Modern inner model theory, due to Steel, Mitchell, and Woodin, constructs mice (iterable premice) that serve as building blocks for models with superstrong, Woodin, and supercompact cardinals. The ultimate goal is the “ultimate inner model” that would accommodate all large cardinals and resolve the continuum problem from within a canonical universe.

Worked Example: Forcing a Cohen Real
Let ℙ be the poset of finite partial functions p: ω → 2 ordered by reverse inclusion (q ≤ p iff q ⊇ p). Show that if G is ℙ‑generic over V, then the union ⋃G is a total function f: ω → 2 and f ∉ V.
Each condition p ∈ ℙ is a finite function. For any n ∈ ω, the set D_n = {p ∈ ℙ : n ∈ dom(p)} is dense in ℙ and belongs to V. Since G meets every dense set in V, there is p_n ∈ G ∩ D_n. Because G is a filter, the conditions are compatible, so the union f = ⋃G is a function with domain ω. For each n, f(n) = p_n(n) ∈ {0,1}, so f: ω → 2. If f were in V, then the set E = {p ∈ ℙ : p ⊈ f} would be dense (any condition can be extended to disagree with f on a new coordinate). But G ∩ E = ∅ because every p ∈ G is a subset of f. This contradicts genericity. Hence f ∉ V.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a forcing construction, first identify the poset and the dense sets that guarantee the desired property. Write down the definition of genericity and verify that the generic filter meets each dense set. For inner model questions, recall the condensation lemma and the covering lemma; they are the standard tools for proving that a set is constructible or that a cardinal is preserved. Keep the distinction between symmetric submodels (for AC independence) and full generic extensions (for CH independence) clear.

Determinacy, Projective Sets, and Large Cardinals

Infinite two‑player games of perfect information on ω provide a natural setting for determinacy. A game G(A) with payoff set A ⊆ ω^ω is determined if one player has a winning strategy. Gale and Stewart (1953) proved that all open (and closed) games are determined. Martin (1975) established Borel determinacy: every Borel subset of ω^ω yields a determined game. The proof uses a transfinite induction on the Borel rank and requires the existence of iterated power sets up to ω₁, hence it cannot be carried out in Zermelo set theory alone. Projective determinacy (PD) asserts that every projective set (Σ1_n, Π1_n) is determined. Martin and Steel (1989) showed that PD follows from the existence of infinitely many Woodin cardinals. Conversely, Woodin proved that PD implies the existence of inner models with infinitely many Woodin cardinals. The Axiom of Determinacy (AD) states that all subsets of ω^ω are determined; AD contradicts the full Axiom of Choice but holds in L(ℝ) under large cardinal assumptions. In L(ℝ), AD is equivalent to the existence of infinitely many Woodin cardinals with a measurable above them (Woodin, 1988). Determinacy has profound regularity consequences: all projective sets are Lebesgue measurable, have the Baire property, and the perfect set property. The hierarchy of determinacy axioms calibrates the consistency strength of regularity properties for definable sets of reals and links descriptive set theory directly to the large cardinal hierarchy.

Reflection Principles and the Levy Hierarchy

The Lévy hierarchy classifies formulas of set theory by the complexity of their quantifiers: Σ₀ = Π₀ = Δ₀ are bounded formulas; Σn+1 formulas are of the form ∃x φ with φ ∈ Π_n; Πn+1 formulas are ∀x φ with φ ∈ Σ_n. The Reflection Theorem (Montague–Lévy, 1961) states that for any finite set of formulas Φ, there is a club class of ordinals α such that ⟨V_α,∈⟩ is an elementary substructure of V for all formulas in Φ. In particular, for each n there is a proper class of Σ_n‑correct cardinals κ (V_κ ≺Σ_n V). Reflection is provable in ZFC and is a key tool for constructing inner models and proving consistency results. A cardinal κ is Π^m_n‑indescribable if for every Π^m_n sentence φ and every A ⊆ V_κ, ⟨V_κ,∈,A⟩ ⊨ φ implies there is α < κ with ⟨V_α,∈,A∩V_α⟩ ⊨ φ. Indescribability strengthens reflection by allowing second‑order parameters. Π11‑indescribable cardinals are exactly the weakly compact cardinals. Higher indescribability corresponds to larger large cardinals: Π^m_n‑indescribable cardinals sit below measurable cardinals for m≥2. The Lévy hierarchy also underlies the definition of the constructible hierarchy L_α and the fine‑structure projecta. In proof theory, the ordinal analysis of theories like Kripke–Platek set theory (KP) uses Σ₁‑reflection to assign proof‑theoretic ordinals. Reflection principles thus bridge the gap between syntactic complexity, large cardinal combinatorics, and the structure of the cumulative hierarchy.

Ordinal Analysis and Proof‑Theoretic Strength

Ordinal analysis assigns to each formal theory T a proof‑theoretic ordinal |T|, the supremum of the order types of primitive recursive well‑orderings that T can prove are well‑founded. Gentzen (1936) showed that Peano Arithmetic (PA) has proof‑theoretic ordinal ε₀, the least ordinal closed under ω‑exponentiation. The consistency of PA is provable in primitive recursive arithmetic plus transfinite induction up to ε₀. For stronger theories, the ordinals grow rapidly: the system ATR₀ (arithmetical transfinite recursion) has ordinal Γ₀ (the Feferman–Schütte ordinal), while Π¹₁‑CA₀ reaches the Takeuti–Feferman–Buchholz ordinal ψ₀(Ω_ω). The ordinal analysis of Kripke–Platek set theory with Σ₁‑separation (KP) yields the Bachmann–Howard ordinal. Adding Π₃‑reflection to KP reaches the ordinal of Π¹₂‑CA₀. Large cardinal axioms correspond to even larger ordinals via ordinal collapsing functions: the existence of a measurable cardinal implies the well‑foundedness of the ordinal ψ(Ω_ω) in a suitable notation system. Rathjen and others have developed ordinal analyses for theories with Mahlo, weakly compact, and Π^m_n‑indescribable cardinals, using infinitary proof systems and operator‑controlled derivations. The program of ordinal analysis provides a precise calibration of the consistency strength of mathematical theories and reveals the deep connection between proof theory, large cardinals, and the structure of the constructible hierarchy.

  • Confusing forcing with symmetric models: forcing adds generic sets, but independence of AC requires symmetric submodels, not the full generic extension.
  • Assuming L satisfies CH but not GCH: Gödel proved L satisfies GCH, so CH holds automatically in L.
  • Thinking Borel determinacy is provable in ZF alone: Martin’s proof uses replacement up to ω₁, so it needs ZFC or at least Zermelo + Σ₁‑replacement.
  • Equating projective determinacy with AD: PD only covers projective sets, while AD asserts determinacy for all sets of reals and contradicts AC.
  • Misapplying the reflection theorem: reflection gives Σ_n‑correct cardinals, but not every Σ_n‑correct cardinal is inaccessible; additional closure properties are needed.
  • Overlooking the role of ordinal collapsing functions in proof theory: the proof‑theoretic ordinal of a theory with large cardinals is not the large cardinal itself but a recursive ordinal obtained by collapsing.
  • Review these traps carefully before the exam.

Forcing Axioms and the Structure of the Continuum

Forcing axioms assert that certain families of dense sets in a partial order admit a filter meeting all of them. Martin's Axiom MA(κ) states that for any ccc partial order ℙ and any family 𝒟 of ≤ κ dense subsets of ℙ, there is a filter 𝐺 ⊆ ℙ intersecting every member of 𝒟. MA(ℵ₁) is equivalent to MA for all ccc posets and implies 2^ℵ₀ > ℵ₁; in fact MA(κ) holds for all κ < 2^ℵ₀. The Proper Forcing Axiom PFA, introduced by Baumgartner, replaces ccc with proper forcing — those preserving stationary subsets of ω₁. PFA implies 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂, the Singular Cardinals Hypothesis, and that every Aronszajn tree is special. Martin's Maximum MM, due to Foreman, Magidor, and Shelah (1988), extends PFA to all posets preserving stationary subsets of ω₁; MM implies 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂ and that the nonstationary ideal on ω₁ is ℵ₂-saturated. The consistency strength of PFA is a supercompact cardinal; MM requires a supercompact cardinal as well. Forcing axioms decide many cardinal invariants of the continuum: under PFA, 𝔭 = 𝔱 = ℵ₂, 𝔟 = 𝔡 = ℵ₂, add(ℳ) = cov(ℳ) = ℵ₂, while 𝔞 = ℵ₁ remains independent. The hierarchy MA < PFA < MM calibrates the tension between combinatorial principles and the size of the continuum, and their equiconsistency with large cardinals anchors them in the consistency strength hierarchy.

Inner Model Theory and Core Models

Inner model theory constructs canonical transitive models of ZFC containing all ordinals, approximating V from below. The core model K, developed by Jensen, Dodd, Mitchell, and Steel, is the maximal iterable inner model not reaching a measurable cardinal. Below a measurable, K exists and satisfies the Covering Lemma: for every uncountable set X of ordinals, there is Y ∈ K with X ⊆ Y and |Y| = |X|. This fails at a measurable, where 0^♯ exists and K = L[0^♯]. For larger large cardinals, one builds mice — iterable premice with extenders. A premouse is a structure ⟨J_α[𝐸], ∈, 𝐸⟩ where 𝐸 codes extender sequences; iterability means all iteration trees have well-founded models. The core model K^DJ for a Woodin cardinal uses the Dodd-Jensen property to compare mice. Steel's core model induction shows that determinacy hypotheses imply the existence of mice with Woodin cardinals. The comparison lemma for mice (Mitchell-Steel) states that any two iterable mice are comparable via iteration. The hierarchy of core models K, K^DJ, K^c, … calibrates consistency strength: if there is no inner model with a Woodin cardinal, then K^DJ exists and satisfies covering for Σ₂ formulas. The fine structure of mice — projecta, standard parameters, solidity — mirrors the fine structure of L but with extenders replacing the Σ₁-Skolem functions. Inner model theory thus provides the "lower bounds" for consistency strength, while forcing provides "upper bounds"; their meeting at equiconsistency results (e.g., PFA ⇔ supercompact) completes the calibration.

Worked Comparison: MA vs PFA vs MM
State the exact consistency strength of each forcing axiom and one cardinal invariant it decides differently from the others.
MA(ℵ₁) is equiconsistent with ZFC (no large cardinals needed); it implies 𝔭 = 𝔱 = ℵ₁ and 2^ℵ₀ > ℵ₁ but does not fix 2^ℵ₀. PFA is equiconsistent with a supercompact cardinal; it implies 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂ and 𝔭 = 𝔱 = ℵ₂. MM is also equiconsistent with a supercompact cardinal (but strictly stronger than PFA in direct implication); it implies 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂ and that the nonstationary ideal on ω₁ is ℵ₂-saturated, which PFA does not decide. The key difference: MA is a ccc axiom consistent with CH failing arbitrarily high; PFA and MM fix the continuum at ℵ₂ and require large cardinals.
Exam Strategy: Forcing Axiom Hierarchy
Memorise the triplet: MA (ccc, no large cardinals, continuum flexible) < PFA (proper, supercompact, 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂) < MM (stationary-preserving, supercompact, NS_ω₁ saturated). Examiners often ask which axiom implies the Singular Cardinals Hypothesis (PFA and MM do; MA does not) or which decides the value of 𝔭 (PFA and MM give ℵ₂; MA gives ℵ₁). Link each axiom to its large cardinal equiconsistency — this is a standard "match the following" question type.

Descriptive Set Theory: Scales, Uniformization, and the Projective Hierarchy

The projective hierarchy classifies subsets of Polish spaces by quantifier complexity over ℝ: Σ¹₁ (analytic), Π¹₁ (coanalytic), Σ¹ₙ₊₁ = ∃^ℝ Π¹ₙ, Π¹ₙ₊₁ = ∀^ℝ Σ¹ₙ. A scale on a set A ⊆ X is a sequence of norms φₙ: A → Ord such that if xₖ → x and φₙ(xₖ) is eventually constant for each n, then x ∈ A. The Scale Property for a pointclass Γ means every A ∈ Γ admits a Γ-scale. Under Projective Determinacy PD, every projective set has the scale property (Moschovakis, 1971). Scales yield uniformization: if A ⊆ X × Y is in Γ and Γ has the scale property with appropriate closure, then A admits a uniformizing function in Γ. The Moschovakis Coding Lemma states that under AD, every Σ¹₂ set of reals can be coded by a real. The Wadge hierarchy refines the projective hierarchy by continuous reducibility: A ≤_W B iff A = f⁻¹(B) for continuous f. Under AD, the Wadge hierarchy of subsets of ω^ω is well-ordered of length Θ, the supremum of ordinals surjecting onto ℝ. The periodicity theorems (Martin-Monk, Steel) show that the Wadge degrees of Σ¹₂ₙ₊₁ and Π¹₂ₙ₊₁ alternate in a pattern determined by the projective ordinals δ¹ₙ. The projective ordinals δ¹ₙ = sup{length of Δ¹ₙ prewellorderings} satisfy δ¹₁ = ω₁, δ¹₂ = ω₂ under AD, and δ¹ₙ are the Suslin cardinals. The connection to large cardinals: PD is equiconsistent with infinitely many Woodin cardinals (Martin-Steel, Woodin). The scale property for Σ¹ₙ₊₁ is equivalent to the existence of a Σ¹ₙ₊₁ wellordering of ℝ, which under AD has length δ¹ₙ₊₁. Descriptive set theory thus translates determinacy into structural regularity properties — measurability, Baire property, perfect set property — and calibrates them via the projective ordinals and Wadge degrees.

Reverse Mathematics and Subsystems of Second-Order Arithmetic

Reverse mathematics, initiated by Friedman and Simpson, calibrates the logical strength of ordinary mathematical theorems by identifying the weakest subsystem of second-order arithmetic proving them. The base system RCA₀ (Recursive Comprehension Axiom) has Δ⁰₁-comprehension and Σ⁰₁-induction; its ω-models are exactly the Turing ideals. WKL₀ adds Weak König's Lemma (every infinite binary tree has a path); it is equivalent to Heine-Borel compactness of [0,1], the existence of separating hyperplanes, and the Gödel Completeness Theorem for countable languages. ACA₀ adds arithmetical comprehension; it is equivalent to the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, the existence of algebraic closures of countable fields, and the sequential completeness of ℝ. ATR₀ (Arithmetical Transfinite Recursion) allows iteration of arithmetical comprehension along any well-ordering; it is equivalent to the comparability of countable well-orderings, the existence of Σ¹₁-separating sets, and the open determinacy for countable games. Π¹₁-CA₀ adds Π¹₁-comprehension; it is equivalent to the Cantor-Bendixson theorem for closed sets, the existence of countable coded ω-models of ACA₀, and the determinacy of Π¹₁ games. The ordinal analysis of these systems: |RCA₀| = ω^ω, |WKL₀| = ω^ω, |ACA₀| = ε₀, |ATR₀| = Γ₀ (Feferman-Schütte), |Π¹₁-CA₀| = ψ₀(Ω_ω) (Takeuti-Feferman-Buchholz). The equivalence theorems are proved over RCA₀: e.g., "Every countable vector space has a basis" ⇔ ACA₀; "Every countable abelian group is a direct sum of a divisible group and a reduced group" ⇔ ACA₀; "The Hahn-Banach theorem for separable spaces" ⇔ WKL₀. Reverse mathematics thus maps the landscape of countable mathematics onto a hierarchy of five "Big Five" systems, with recent work exploring the "zoo" of principles between them (RT²₂, COH, SADS, etc.).

Cardinal Invariants of the Continuum and PCF Theory

The cardinal invariants of the continuum measure the combinatorial structure of (ω^ω, ≤*) and the ideal of meager/null sets. The dominating number 𝔡 = min{|F| : F ⊆ ω^ω dominating}, the bounding number 𝔟 = min{|F| : F ⊆ ω^ω unbounded}, the splitting number 𝔰 = min{|S| : S ⊆ [ω]^ω splitting all infinite sets}, the reaping number 𝔯 = min{|R| : R ⊆ [ω]^ω unsplit}, the almost disjointness number 𝔞 = max{|A| : A ⊆ [ω]^ω almost disjoint}, the pseudointersection number 𝔭 = min{|F| : F ⊆ [ω]^ω centred, no pseudointersection}, and the tower number 𝔱 = min{length of a tower in ([ω]^ω, ⊆*)}. ZFC proves ℵ₁ ≤ 𝔭 ≤ 𝔱 ≤ 𝔥 ≤ 𝔤 ≤ 𝔡 ≤ 𝔠 and ℵ₁ ≤ 𝔟 ≤ 𝔡 ≤ 𝔠, with 𝔭 ≤ 𝔟, 𝔱 ≤ 𝔡. The Cichoń diagram relates measure and category invariants: add(ℳ) ≤ cov(ℳ) ≤ 𝔡 ≤ cof(ℳ) ≤ 𝔠 and add(𝒩) ≤ cov(𝒩) ≤ 𝔡 ≤ cof(𝒩) ≤ 𝔠, with add(ℳ) ≤ add(𝒩) and cof(𝒩) ≤ cof(ℳ). Shelah's PCF (Possible Cofinalities) theory analyses the structure of ∏i<κ λ_i / J for singular λ = sup λ_i. The fundamental theorem: for any progressive set 𝔞 of regular cardinals, pcf(𝔞) has a maximum and |pcf(𝔞)| < |𝔞|⁺⁴. The cov vs pp theorem: cov(λ, κ, θ, σ) = sup{pp(μ) : μ ∈ pcf(𝔞)} for suitable 𝔞. PCF yields the bound 2^ℵ_ω < ℵω₄ (Shelah, 1994), improving the Galvin-Hajnal bound. The invariant 𝔭 = 𝔱 was proved by Malliaris and Shelah (2016), resolving a decades-old problem. The consistency of all Cichoń's diagram invariants being pairwise distinct was shown by Goldstern, Kellner, and Shelah (2019) using a finite support iteration of ccc posets. PCF theory thus provides the deep structural engine behind the independence results for cardinal invariants, linking singular cardinal arithmetic to the combinatorics of the continuum.

Models of Set Theory without the Axiom of Choice

Symmetric models, introduced by Cohen and refined by Jech-Sochor, produce models of ZF + ¬AC by taking a forcing extension V[G] and restricting to the class HS of hereditarily symmetric names. A name τ is symmetric if its symmetry group sym(τ) = {π ∈ Aut(ℙ) : πτ = τ} belongs to a normal filter ℱ of subgroups of Aut(ℙ); τ is hereditarily symmetric if all names in its transitive closure are symmetric. The basic Fraenkel model adds a countable set of Cohen reals with the finite-support permutation group and the filter of subgroups fixing finite sets; the resulting symmetric model satisfies ZF + "there is an infinite Dedekind-finite set of reals" + ¬AC_ω. The Feferman-Levy model collapses ℵ_ω to ℵ₁ using a symmetric collapse, yielding ZF + ℝ is a countable union of countable sets + ¬AC_ω(ℝ). Solovay's model (1970) starts with an inaccessible κ, collapses it to ω₁ via Levy collapse, and takes the symmetric submodel of sets hereditarily definable from ordinals and reals; it satisfies ZF + DC + "every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable, has the Baire property, and the perfect set property". The Axiom of Determinacy AD holds in L(ℝ) under large cardinals (Woodin), and AD implies ¬AC but DC_ℝ. The HOD (hereditarily ordinal-definable sets) of a model of AD is a model of ZFC with a proper class of Woodin cardinals. The hierarchy of choice principles: AC ⇒ DC ⇒ AC_ω ⇒ AC_fin; none reverse in ZF. The Kinna-Wagner principle (every set embeds into a power set of a well-ordered set) is equivalent to AC. The study of ZF models reveals the precise choice strength needed for analysis: Hahn-Banach ⇔ BPI (Boolean Prime Ideal theorem) ⇔ Compactness for propositional logic; Tychonoff for Hausdorff spaces ⇔ BPI; Tychonoff for all spaces ⇔ AC. The interplay between symmetric models, inner models of determinacy, and forcing over ZF maps the geography of choice-free mathematics.

  • Confusing the consistency strength of MA (none) with PFA/MM (supercompact) — MA is a theorem of ZFC for κ < 2^ℵ₀, while PFA/MM require large cardinals.
  • Thinking the core model K exists above a measurable cardinal — K exists only below the first measurable; above it, 0^♯ exists and K = L[0^♯].
  • Equating the scale property with uniformization — scales imply uniformization only for pointclasses closed under ∃^ℝ and ∀^ℝ with appropriate coding.
  • Assuming WKL₀ proves the existence of a non-principal ultrafilter on ω — WKL₀ is conservative over RCA₀ for Π¹₁ sentences and does not prove the existence of any non-computable set.
  • Believing all cardinal invariants in Cichoń's diagram can be simultaneously distinct in ZFC — this is a consistency result (Goldstern-Kellner-Shelah), not a theorem of ZFC.
  • Thinking Solovay's model satisfies full AC — it satisfies DC but not AC_ω(ℝ); the reals cannot be well-ordered there.
  • Overlooking that PCF theory applies to singular cardinals of uncountable cofinality — the bound 2^ℵ_ω < ℵω₄ uses the structure of pcf(𝔞) for 𝔞 = {ℵ_n : n < ω}.

hand/measure-theory.html:
Carathéodory’s Extension Theorem – From Pre‑Measures to Full Measures

The construction of Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ is a special case of a far more general result: given a set X and an algebra 𝔄 of subsets of X, a function μ₀:𝔄→[0,∞] that is countably additive on disjoint families whose union stays in 𝔄 is called a pre‑measure. Carathéodory’s extension theorem guarantees that such a μ₀ extends uniquely to a complete measure μ on the σ‑algebra σ(𝔄) generated by 𝔄, provided μ₀ is σ‑finite (i.e., X can be written as a countable union of sets of finite μ₀‑measure). The proof proceeds by defining an outer measure μ* on all subsets of X via

μ*(E)=inf{∑ μ₀(A_i) : E⊂⋃A_i, A_i∈𝔄}. A set E is declared μ*-measurable if for every A⊂X, μ*(A)=μ*(A∩E)+μ*(A∖E). The collection of μ*-measurable sets forms a σ‑algebra containing 𝔄, and the restriction of μ* to this σ‑algebra is a complete measure extending μ₀.

Why this matters for exam‑level problems:

  • When asked to construct a measure on a product space, candidates often start from rectangles and invoke Carathéodory to justify the existence of the product measure without re‑proving countable additivity.
  • In probability, the theorem underlies the definition of distributions from cumulative distribution functions (CDFs). The CDF F defines a pre‑measure on half‑open intervals (a,b] by μ₀((a,b])=F(b)−F(a); Carathéodory then yields the Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure associated with F.
  • σ‑finiteness is a frequent exam trap: if the pre‑measure is not σ‑finite, the extension may fail to be unique. Classic counter‑examples involve counting measure on an uncountable set.

Typical exam question: “Show that the counting pre‑measure on the algebra of finite subsets of an uncountable set X does not extend uniquely to a measure on the power set of X.” The answer hinges on the lack of σ‑finiteness, leading to many non‑equivalent extensions (e.g., the trivial extension that assigns ∞ to every infinite set).

Completion of Measure Spaces and Lebesgue–Stieltjes Measures

Even after Carathéodory’s theorem, a measure space (X,𝔽,μ) may miss subsets of null sets. The completion of (X,𝔽,μ) adds every subset N⊂Z where Z∈𝔽 and μ(Z)=0, forming the σ‑algebra

𝔽̂ = {A∪N : A∈𝔽, N⊂Z for some Z∈𝔽 with μ(Z)=0}.

On 𝔽̂ we define μ̂(A∪N)=μ(A). The resulting space (X,𝔽̂,μ̂) is complete: every μ̂‑null set is in 𝔽̂. Completion is essential when dealing with Lebesgue integration, because many limit processes produce sets that differ from measurable sets only by a null set.

Lebesgue–Stieltjes measures illustrate the interplay of CDFs, pre‑measures, and completion. Given a right‑continuous, non‑decreasing function F:ℝ→ℝ, define μ₀ on half‑open intervals (a,b] by μ₀((a,b])=F(b)−F(a). Carathéodory extends μ₀ to a measure μ_F on the Borel σ‑algebra. However, μ_F may assign zero measure to a Borel set B while a subset N⊂B is not Borel. After completion, N becomes measurable with μ̂_F(N)=0, allowing us to integrate functions that are only defined up to sets of μ_F‑measure zero.

Exam‑level nuance: when a problem states “let X be a random variable with distribution function F,” the implicit measure is the completed Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure. Ignoring completion can lead to incorrect statements about almost sure convergence, because convergence “a.s.” is defined with respect to the completed σ‑algebra.

Important historical note: the Lebesgue–Stieltjes construction was formalised by Henri Lebesgue (1902) and later refined by Thomas Joannes Stieltjes (1894) in the context of continued fractions. Their combined legacy provides the rigorous foundation for probability densities, discrete mass points, and mixed distributions.

Technique – Using Completion to Resolve a Measurability Issue
Let μ be Lebesgue measure on ℝ and let A⊂[0,1] be a non‑Borel set of Lebesgue measure zero (such sets exist by the axiom of choice). Define f(x)=1_A(x). Show that f is μ‑integrable and compute ∫ f dμ.
Since A has outer measure zero, μ*(A)=0. In the completed measure space (ℝ,𝔏̂,μ̂), every subset of A is measurable with μ̂‑measure zero. Hence f is measurable (its pre‑image of {1} is A, a μ̂‑null set). The integral of a non‑negative simple function equals the sum of values times the measure of the level sets: ∫ f dμ̂ = 1·μ̂(A)=0. Therefore f is integrable and its integral is 0, even though A is not Borel.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions “almost surely” or “with probability 1,” immediately check whether the underlying σ‑algebra has been completed. If the problem involves a set defined via a limit (e.g., lim sup of events), assume completion; this avoids losing marks for claiming a set is non‑measurable.

Uniform Integrability and the de la Vallée‑Poussin Criterion

Uniform integrability (UI) is the bridge between convergence in measure and convergence in L¹. A family 𝔉⊂L¹(μ) is uniformly integrable if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that μ(A)<δ implies supf∈𝔉∫_A|f| dμ<ε. Intuitively, UI prevents “mass” from escaping to sets of arbitrarily small measure.

The de la Vallée‑Poussin theorem provides a practical test: 𝔉 is UI iff there exists a convex, increasing function Φ:[0,∞)→[0,∞) with Φ(t)/t→∞ as t→∞ such that supf∈𝔉∫ Φ(|f|) dμ < ∞. Common choices are Φ(t)=t·log(1+t) or Φ(t)=t^p for p>1.

Why UI appears in exams:

  • In the Vitali convergence theorem, the hypothesis “{f_n} is uniformly integrable and f_n→f in measure” yields f_n→f in L¹. Many problems ask to verify UI for a given sequence, often by exhibiting a suitable Φ.
  • In probability, UI of {X_n} is equivalent to the family {E[|X_n|]} being bounded and the tails being uniformly small. This is the key condition in the proof of the dominated convergence theorem for expectations.
  • UI also characterises relatively compact subsets of L¹ (Dunford–Pettis theorem). Exam questions may request a proof that a set is relatively compact by showing UI and tightness.

Typical trap: confusing “bounded in L¹” with UI. A sequence with ‖f_n‖₁≤C need not be UI; for example, f_n=n·χ[0,1/n] has constant L¹ norm 1 but fails UI because the mass concentrates on shrinking intervals.

Sample calculation: Let f_n(x)=n·χ[0,1/n] on [0,1] with Lebesgue measure. Choose Φ(t)=t·log(1+t). Then ∫ Φ(|f_n|) = ∫01/n n·log(1+n) dx = (1/n)·n·log(1+n)=log(1+n)→∞, so the de la Vallée‑Poussin condition fails, confirming non‑UI.

Martingale Convergence Theorem via Measure‑Theoretic Tools

Martingales are sequences {X_n} of integrable random variables adapted to an increasing filtration {𝔽_n} such that E[Xn+1|𝔽_n]=X_n a.s. The martingale convergence theorem (MCT) states: if {X_n} is a martingale that is uniformly integrable, then X_n converges a.s. and in L¹ to a limit X∞, and X∞=E[X∞|𝔽_n] for all n.

Measure‑theoretic proof outline:

  1. Define the maximal function X* = sup_n |X_n|. Doob’s maximal inequality gives μ({X*>λ}) ≤ (1/λ)·sup_n E[|X_n|] for λ>0. This inequality is derived from the sub‑martingale property of |X_n| and the optional stopping theorem.
  2. Uniform integrability of {X_n} implies that {X*} is integrable. Consequently, X*<∞ a.s., establishing almost sure boundedness of the martingale.
  3. Apply the upcrossing lemma: for any a+]−E[(X0−a)+])/(b−a). Uniform integrability forces the total expected upcrossings to be finite, which forces the limit limn→∞ X_n to exist a.s.
  4. Finally, the UI condition guarantees convergence in L¹ by the Vitali convergence theorem (a corollary of UI and a.e. convergence).

Exam relevance:

  • Problems often ask to verify the UI condition for a given martingale. Typical techniques include bounding moments (e.g., showing sup_n E[|X_n|^p] < ∞ for some p>1) and invoking the de la Vallée‑Poussin criterion.
  • In discrete‑time gambling models, the optional stopping theorem is used to compute expectations of stopped martingales; the measure‑theoretic justification rests on the σ‑algebra of the stopping time.
  • When the filtration is generated by a sequence of independent random variables, the martingale difference sequence D_n = X_n−Xn-1 often satisfies E[D_n|𝔽n-1]=0, making {X_n} a martingale. Proving convergence then reduces to checking UI of the partial sums.

Common mistake: assuming that any L²‑bounded martingale automatically converges a.s. While L²‑boundedness implies UI (by Cauchy–Schwarz), the exam setter may deliberately give a martingale that is only L¹‑bounded to test whether the candidate recognises the need for UI.

Weak Convergence of Measures, Prokhorov’s Theorem and Applications

Weak convergence (also called convergence in distribution) of probability measures μ_n→μ on a metric space (S,d) is defined by the convergence of integrals of bounded continuous functions:

μ_n ⇒ μ ⇔ ∀ f∈C_b(S), ∫ f dμ_n → ∫ f dμ.

Key characterisation tools:

  • Portmanteau theorem provides equivalent formulations: convergence of μ_n(A) for all continuity sets A, limsup inequality for closed sets, liminf for open sets, and convergence of characteristic functions when S=ℝ^k.
  • Prokhorov’s theorem links tightness and relative compactness: a family {μ_n} on a complete separable metric space (Polish space) is relatively compact in the weak topology iff it is tight, i.e., for every ε>0 there exists a compact K⊂S with μ_n(K)≥1−ε for all n.

Application to the Central Limit Theorem (CLT): Let S_n = (X₁+…+X_n)/√n where {X_i} are i.i.d. with mean 0, variance 1. The sequence of distributions μ_n of S_n is tight (by Chebyshev’s inequality) and any weak limit must have characteristic function φ(t)=e−t²/2. By Lévy’s continuity theorem, μ_n ⇒ N(0,1). The measure‑theoretic proof hinges on tightness (Prokhorov) and pointwise convergence of characteristic functions.

Exam scenarios:

  1. Given a sequence of distributions defined by densities f_n(x)=n·e−nx·χ[0,∞)(x), identify the weak limit. The densities concentrate near 0; using the change of variable y=nx shows μ_n ⇒ δ₀ (Dirac measure at 0). The candidate must justify tightness and verify convergence on continuity sets.
  2. In a problem on empirical measures, one is asked to prove that the empirical distribution of i.i.d. samples converges weakly to the true distribution almost surely (Glivenko–Cantelli). The proof uses the law of large numbers for indicator functions of continuity sets and then invokes the Portmanteau theorem.
  3. When a question mentions “the sequence {μ_n} is uniformly tight,” the examiner expects the candidate to invoke Prokhorov to claim existence of a weakly convergent subsequence, then identify the limit using additional information (e.g., moments or characteristic functions).

Typical trap: confusing weak convergence with convergence of densities in L¹. Weak convergence does not require the densities to converge pointwise or in norm; only the integrals against bounded continuous test functions must converge. Candidates who attempt to integrate the densities directly often miss the role of tightness.

  • Assuming σ‑finiteness automatically guarantees uniqueness of Carathéodory extensions; neglect the counter‑example of counting measure on an uncountable set.
  • Overlooking completion when a problem involves “almost everywhere” statements; forgetting that subsets of null sets become measurable only after completion.
  • Equating boundedness in L¹ with uniform integrability; the classic counter‑example f_n=n·χ[0,1/n] must be remembered.
  • Skipping the verification of UI in martingale convergence problems; L²‑boundedness is sufficient but not necessary, and the exam may present only L¹ bounds.
  • Treating weak convergence of measures as pointwise convergence of densities; always revert to the Portmanteau criteria or characteristic functions.
  • Neglecting tightness when applying Prokhorov’s theorem; without a tightness argument the existence of a weak limit cannot be claimed.
  • Misapplying the optional stopping theorem without checking the integrability of the stopped martingale; the theorem requires the stopped variable to be integrable.

Differentiation of Measures and the Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem

The Lebesgue differentiation theorem states that for any locally integrable function f on ℝⁿ, the average of f over balls centred at x converges to f(x) for almost every x as the radius tends to zero. Formally, if B(x,r) denotes the open ball of radius r, then

limr→0 (1/|B(x,r)|) ∫B(x,r) f(y) dy = f(x) for a.e. x.

The proof rests on the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function Mf(x) = supr>0 (1/|B(x,r)|) ∫B(x,r) |f(y)| dy. The maximal inequality ‖Mf‖L¹,∞ ≤ C‖f‖L¹ yields a weak‑type (1,1) bound, which together with density of continuous functions in L¹ gives almost‑everywhere convergence. A key corollary is the Lebesgue density theorem: for any measurable set E, the density limr→0 |E∩B(x,r)|/|B(x,r)| equals 1 for a.e. x∈E and 0 for a.e. x∉E. This theorem underpins the identification of points of density with the support of a measure and is essential when proving that a Radon–Nikodym derivative can be recovered by differentiating the corresponding measure.

In the language of measures, if μ is a finite Borel measure on ℝⁿ absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure λ, the Radon–Nikodym derivative dμ/dλ coincides λ‑a.e. with the limit of μ(B(x,r))/λ(B(x,r)). For singular measures the limit is either 0 or ∞ λ‑a.e., reflecting the mutual singularity. Examiners often ask to distinguish between the behaviour of absolutely continuous and singular parts via differentiation, or to apply the density theorem to show that a set of positive measure contains points of density 1.

Conditional Expectation as a Radon–Nikodym Derivative

Let (Ω,ℱ,ℙ) be a probability space and 𝒢⊂ℱ a sub‑σ‑algebra. For an integrable random variable X, the conditional expectation E[X|𝒢] is the unique (up to ℙ‑a.s. equality) 𝒢‑measurable random variable Y satisfying ∫A Y dℙ = ∫A X dℙ for every A∈𝒢. This definition is precisely the Radon–Nikodym derivative of the signed measure ν(A)=∫A X dℙ with respect to ℙ restricted to 𝒢. The existence of Y follows from the Radon–Nikodym theorem because ν≪ℙ on 𝒢 and both are σ‑finite.

Properties such as linearity, tower property E[E[X|𝒢]|ℋ]=E[X|ℋ] for ℋ⊂𝒢, and Jensen’s inequality for convex φ (φ(E[X|𝒢]) ≤ E[φ(X)|𝒢]) are direct consequences of the measure‑theoretic construction. The martingale convergence theorem can be proved by viewing a martingale (Xₙ) as a sequence of Radon–Nikodym derivatives dμₙ/dℙ on an increasing filtration; uniform integrability of {Xₙ} is equivalent to the uniform absolute continuity of the measures μₙ, which in turn yields convergence of the derivatives in L¹.

In exam problems, candidates are frequently asked to compute E[X|𝒢] when 𝒢 is generated by a countable partition {Aₖ}. The answer is Σₖ (∫Aₖ X dℙ / ℙ(Aₖ)) 1Aₖ, provided ℙ(Aₖ)>0. When 𝒢 is generated by a random variable Y, the conditional expectation becomes a Borel function g(Y) where g(y)=E[X|Y=y] is defined via the regular conditional distribution. Recognising the Radon–Nikodym viewpoint avoids the common mistake of treating conditional expectation as an elementary average without verifying 𝒢‑measurability and the defining integral identity.

Worked Example: Conditional Expectation on a Partition
Let Ω={1,2,3,4} with ℙ({i})=1/4. Define X(i)=i². Let 𝒢 be the σ‑algebra generated by the partition {{1,2},{3,4}}. Compute E[X|𝒢].
For A₁={1,2}, ∫A₁ X dℙ = (1²+2²)/4 = 5/4. ℙ(A₁)=1/2. Hence the value on A₁ is (5/4)/(1/2)=5/2. For A₂={3,4}, ∫A₂ X dℙ = (3²+4²)/4 = 25/4. ℙ(A₂)=1/2. Value on A₂ = (25/4)/(1/2)=25/2. Therefore E[X|𝒢](ω)=5/2 for ω∈{1,2} and 25/2 for ω∈{3,4}. This function is 𝒢‑measurable and satisfies the defining integral property.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for a conditional expectation, first identify the generating σ‑algebra. If it is a finite or countable partition, write the explicit formula Σ (∫Aₖ X dℙ)/ℙ(Aₖ) 1Aₖ. For σ‑algebras generated by a random variable, recall that the answer must be a Borel function of that variable; use the regular conditional distribution or the factorisation lemma. Always verify the two defining conditions: 𝒢‑measurability and equality of integrals on every 𝒢‑set.

Singular Continuous Measures and the Cantor–Lebesgue Function

A Borel measure μ on ℝ is singular continuous if it is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure λ (there exists a Borel set N with λ(N)=0 and μ(ℝN)=0) and has no atoms (μ({x})=0 for all x). The canonical example is the Cantor–Lebesgue measure μC supported on the middle‑third Cantor set C. Its distribution function F(x)=μC((−∞,x]) is the Cantor function, also called the Devil’s staircase. F is continuous, non‑decreasing, constant on each interval removed in the construction of C, and satisfies F(0)=0, F(1)=1. Despite being continuous, F′(x)=0 for λ‑a.e. x, yet μC is not absolutely continuous because μC(C)=1 while λ(C)=0.

The Lebesgue decomposition theorem states that any finite Borel measure μ can be uniquely written as μ = μac + μsc + μpp, where μac≪λ, μsc⟂λ and atomless, and μpp is pure point (a countable sum of atoms). The Cantor measure provides the singular continuous component. In Fourier analysis, the Fourier–Stieltjes transform of μC does not vanish at infinity, illustrating that Riemann–Lebesgue lemma fails for singular continuous measures. Examiners may ask to prove that the Cantor function has derivative zero almost everywhere, or to show that a given distribution function corresponds to a singular continuous measure by verifying continuity, absence of jumps, and singularity with respect to λ.

Ergodic Theory: Invariant Measures and the Birkhoff Ergodic Theorem

Let (X,ℬ,μ) be a probability space and T:X→X a measurable transformation preserving μ, i.e. μ(T⁻¹A)=μ(A) for all A∈ℬ. The system is ergodic if every T‑invariant set has measure 0 or 1. The Birkhoff ergodic theorem asserts that for any f∈L¹(μ), the time averages (1/n) Σk=0n−1 f(Tᵏx) converge μ‑a.e. to a T‑invariant function f*. If the system is ergodic, f* is constant μ‑a.e. and equals ∫ f dμ. The proof uses the maximal ergodic inequality: for λ>0, λ μ({supn≥1 (1/n) Σk=0n−1 f(Tᵏx) > λ}) ≤ ∫{f*>λ} f dμ. This inequality is the dynamical analogue of the Hardy–Littlewood maximal inequality and yields almost‑everywhere convergence via a standard density argument.

Applications include the strong law of large numbers for stationary sequences (take T as the shift on the sequence space) and the equidistribution of irrational rotations on the circle (unique ergodicity). In competitive examinations, a typical question presents a measure‑preserving map and asks whether it is ergodic; the candidate must either exhibit a non‑trivial invariant set or invoke a known criterion such as the spectral condition that the only eigenfunctions of the Koopman operator Uf=f∘T with eigenvalue 1 are constants. Another common task is to compute the limit of time averages for a specific observable, which reduces to evaluating the space average when ergodicity is established.

  • Confusing the Lebesgue differentiation theorem with the fundamental theorem of calculus; the former holds for any locally integrable function, the latter requires absolute continuity.
  • Assuming conditional expectation is always given by an elementary formula without checking σ‑finiteness or the defining integral identity.
  • Treating the Cantor function as absolutely continuous because it is continuous; remember that absolute continuity is strictly stronger.
  • Neglecting to verify the maximal ergodic inequality when applying Birkhoff’s theorem; the inequality is the key step that guarantees almost‑everywhere convergence.
  • Misidentifying the singular continuous component in a Lebesgue decomposition; a measure can be singular yet have atoms, so atomlessness must be checked separately.
  • Applying the Radon–Nikodym theorem without confirming absolute continuity; the derivative does not exist if the measure is not absolutely continuous with respect to the reference measure.
  • Overlooking the role of σ‑finiteness in the Radon–Nikodym theorem and in the construction of conditional expectations on non‑probability spaces.

These advanced topics complete the measure‑theoretic toolkit needed for rigorous analysis and probability at the highest competitive level.
